On this page
Compatibility policyRelease gateOptional extensionsBicycle profileBicycle turn windowsBicycle timed edgesBicycle traffic stressBicycle walking accessAdd street names to an existing CityScenario street bases and endpoint overlays
A City written by one VIGO release stays readable by later releases, and every standard City stays readable by the published reference runtime. This page is that promise: the compatibility policy, the release gate that enforces it, and the optional extensions a City may carry. Maintainers must follow it for any change to a reader, a writer or prepared data.


Compatibility policy


The published reference runtime at source c8da84fff7812d570fd5985cbcbcb83885587bf6 is the permanent prepared-data baseline. Future VIGO readers must continue to open these Cities without requiring users to rebuild them. Future standard City writers must continue producing data readable by that published runtime.


Keep the existing City manifest, routing/street SQLite layouts, prepared access and timetable snapshots, CCH members, and portable relative references compatible. Do not reuse a format identifier for an incompatible layout. Algorithm and performance improvements must retain the published representation. Additional optional metadata/indexes are allowed only when existing readers can ignore them and old Cities still work without them. A new required format or an automatic rebuild of valid baseline Cities violates this policy.


This applies to regular, wheelchair and scenario-collection data. It does not promise immutable GTFS/OSM contents or identical answers after a routing bug fix. Invalid/corrupt source data must still be rejected. Internal diagnostic traces are not a persistent data format. Public vigo.*.v1 results retain existing field meanings, units and time conventions; additions must remain optional.


Release gate


npm run check:format-050 builds candidate runtimes and tests both directions:


  • The candidate reader opens the frozen City produced by the published CLI.
  • The published Rust reader opens a City produced by the candidate writer.


Both execute transit, arrive-by, walking, matrix and reach queries. The test is also part of check:standalone, used by the engine and release CI matrices. The original archive-only CI build (run 37885649818) is preserved in the v0.5.0 release under *-baseline-c8da84fff781.tar.gz asset names. Downloads require no GitHub token and do not expire with Actions artifact retention. Every platform retains its original pinned SHA-256; the later, differently packaged reference downloads are not interchangeable with these baseline assets. For offline checks, VIGO_050_REFERENCE_BINARY may point to an extracted package whose manifest, source identity and executable hash are verified.


The small synthetic GTFS/OSM and prepared archive live in test/fixtures/format-0.5.0. Never regenerate that archive, change its pinned hashes, or weaken its expectations to hide an incompatibility. It is a permanent historical reader test, not generated build output. Extend coverage with new fixtures while retaining this baseline. The initial fixture covers regular walking/transit; additional wheelchair, collection and large-network fixtures are still needed before claiming comprehensive format coverage.


The policy is permanent; the tests are evidence for the cases they execute, not a proof that all future code or every possible City is compatible.


Optional extensions


Each extension below is optional: readers that predate it ignore it, and Cities without it keep working without a rebuild. A present but malformed extension fails admission; an absent one keeps the conservative baseline behavior.


ExtensionIdentified byUsed for
Bicycle profilebikeProfileVersion=1Bike Route, Matrix and Reach
Bicycle turn windowsbikeTurnWindowVersion=1Time-dependent turn restrictions
Bicycle timed edgesbikeEdgeWindowVersion=1Time-dependent road access
Bicycle traffic stressbikeStressVersion=1bike.maxLts
Bicycle walking accessbikeWalkAccessWalking to and from the bicycle network
Street namesplace_streets, place_areas tablesNames for map points
Scenario street basesstreets/<osm-sha256>/Shared streets in scenario collections


Bicycle profile


VIGO writers can add bikeProfileVersion=1 metadata and four base tables to street-index.sqlite. They do not change the walking/driving snapshots, required layouts, City version, or existing units. Historical readers ignore them; new readers require them only for Bike Route and Matrix. A missing profile produces a bike-preparation error without rebuilding an old City.


TableColumns
bike_nodesOSM node_id, integer lon_e7, integer lat_e7
bike_edgesfrom_node, to_node, positive distance_cm, OSM way_id, packed attributes
bike_turnsvia_node, from_way, to_way, only_turn flags
bike_way_turnsfrom_way, ordered JSON via_ways, to_way, only_turn flags


Each edge is directed. Length is rounded upward to centimetres. Attribute bits encode road class (0–2), facility (3–4), surface (5–6), dismount (7), incline percent plus 30 (8–13), motor speed in km/h (14–21), and destination access (22); upper bits are reserved. This compact profile stores no tag strings.


The low turn flag bit marks an only_* restriction. For node turns, bits 1 and 2 distinguish same-way U-turn and straight movements; bit 3 makes a conditional-only rule independent of other allowed alternatives. For via-way turns, bit 1 marks that independent conditional rule. Without a timing index, conditional prohibitions apply all day. Optional metadata counts unsupported relation shapes and conditional restrictions. The reference-reader gate also opens a new City containing these bicycle tables.


Bicycle turn windows


An optional bike_turn_windows table is identified by bikeTurnWindowVersion=1. Its columns are turn_table (0 for bike_turns, 1 for bike_way_turns), turn_row (the referenced table's SQLite rowid), start_minute, and end_minute. Row identities must be preserved with this index. Each interval is half-open in a Monday-first local week: 0 <= start_minute < end_minute <= 10080. Intervals for one restriction must not overlap and are limited to 256. A restriction without interval rows applies at all times. Malformed present indexes produce a bicycle-preparation error; absent indexes preserve the conservative baseline behavior.


Writers compile weekly weekday/time ranges and conditional overrides into these intervals. Unrecognized expressions remain conservative. Readers that ignore the index still enforce every retained restriction. The current runtime evaluates node-turn and via-way windows for dated depart-at requests with a known City timezone. Both share one interned schedule pool. No-turn via-way restrictions are checked at the final movement; only-turn restrictions constrain each movement while the mapped sequence is being followed.


Bicycle timed edges


Optional bike_timed_edges and bike_edge_windows tables are identified by bikeEdgeWindowVersion=1. Timed edges have the same five columns and units as bike_edges, plus a positive window_id. Their allowed entry intervals are in bike_edge_windows(window_id,start_minute,end_minute), with the same Monday-first, half-open minute convention and 256-interval limit. Every referenced schedule must exist, and every stored schedule must be referenced. Both tables must be present together. Equal schedules may be shared across edges and directions.


These supplemental edges never replace the conservative meaning of legacy bike_edges. Earlier bicycle readers ignore them. The current runtime admits them only with a usable depart-at date/timezone, evaluates permissions at entry to each directed segment, and permits completion of a segment entered while open. Attribute variants, such as cycling versus dismounting, use separate timed edges. bike_nodes contains their endpoints; old readers may see isolated nodes. The runtime shares one graph across all bicycle preferences and keeps the window lookup sparse. Internal timed-edge and incoming-turn flags reuse reserved bits in memory only; they are never persisted in attributes.


Bicycle traffic stress


bikeStressVersion=1 adds an optional stress INTEGER NOT NULL column to bike_edges and, when present, bike_timed_edges. Bits 0–2 contain an estimated LTS integer 1–4; bit 3 permits walking while pushing the bicycle. All other bits must be zero. Walking permission includes both incident nodes and the direction of the way. The attributes word, table identities and existing units do not change. Older readers may ignore this column. New readers require both the version and valid values before accepting a traffic-stress limit; old Cities without it retain ordinary bicycle routing. The writer removes temporary intersection data before sealing the City. Custom LTS and signal-aware intersection adjustment are compiled into the column, not inferred at runtime.


Bicycle walking access


bikeWalkAccess is a JSON metadata value with version: 1, the adjacent snapshotSuffix (.street-accelerator-v7.bin), and the pedestrian snapshot's identity, nodeCount and edgeCount. It identifies the optional table bike_walk_nodes(bike_node INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, walk_node INTEGER NOT NULL). bike_node is the original OSM node ID in bike_nodes; walk_node is the zero-based vertex index in that exact spatially ordered pedestrian snapshot. The join is built from source IDs, not coordinate equality, before source-table compaction. Walking indexes must be unique, in range, and coordinate-consistent with their bicycle node. A present malformed or mismatched index fails admission.


These links enable bounded access/egress walks on the prepared public pedestrian graph. The runtime shares its existing immutable snapshot; it retains only the node join and query-local walking scratch. Network walks count toward the walking and total-distance limits and supply mapped geometry. Ordinary coordinate snaps remain unverified and use the existing 80 m pedestrian snap ceiling. A nearer pedestrian attachment cannot be skipped to snap to an unrelated bicycle road. Older readers ignore this index; absent metadata preserves legacy bicycle coordinate attachment. Rebuilding from OSM creates the index for older Cities.


Add street names to an existing City


Older Cities may lack the optional place_streets and place_areas tables. Coordinate labels then fall back to nearby transit stops or “Dropped pin”. Use the original OSM PBF to add names without rebuilding the City:


Shell
npm run backfill:project:places -- --city=/path/to/City --osm=/path/to/original.osm.pbf


The command verifies the source against the street store's SHA-256 fingerprint, stages named ways and their nodes in temporary SQLite storage, and commits the two name tables and an optional placeNames metadata receipt together. It does not change the timetable, routing graphs, accelerators, basemap or City manifest. A completed upgrade is a read-only no-op on retry. A missing source, mismatch, cancellation or publication error leaves the previous name tables intact.


Names describe nearby streets, intersections and supported named areas from OSM; they are not verified postal addresses. No external geocoding is required. Current Rust lookups reload when the SQLite database or its WAL changes. Re-enter a coordinate search to refresh already displayed labels. Studio also needs a build containing coordinate-search naming: quit an older running Studio before opening the updated application, because its single-instance lock otherwise keeps the older process active.


Scenario street bases and endpoint overlays


Scenario collections built from the same OSM bytes and preparation profile keep one immutable base under streets/<osm-sha256>/. Public-only Cities retain the existing relative osm directory link. Endpoint-enabled Cities have their own osm/ directory: relative symbolic links point to the common street database and pedestrian snapshot, and hard links expose the same immutable CCH members inside each City for published readers that enforce adjacent-file resolution. Meanwhile, street-index.sqlite.terminal-access-v1.json remains a regular City-local file. Its boundary components depend on that City's timetable stop anchors and must never be copied from another scenario. The existing filenames and formats remain readable by published runtimes. Moving the entire collection preserves its links; copying one City alone still requires including or materializing its referenced base files.


Archives must preserve hard links to retain the storage savings (for example, use tar); a copying/export tool may materialize duplicate CCH files without changing routing results.


The resident runtime identifies the base by the resolved snapshot directory, shares only the immutable graph and hierarchy, and installs the receiving City's endpoint overlay. Overlay heap usage is charged per City, separately from the shared base. check-scenario-endpoint-access.mjs compares distinct-boundary scenarios with separately built Cities, including resident switching, eviction, relocation and optional published-reader checks.

Validation and compatibility
1 min readSource
On this page
Supported operationsPlatform and build recordsRun the checks
vigo capabilities describes the executable you run.


Supported operations


OperationModes and coverage
Route and MatrixTransit, walk, drive and bike; depart-at and arrive-by
ReachTransit, walk, drive and bike; depart-at and arrive-by
ScenariosReach with exclusions, planned services or compiled overlays; transit Route with exclusions and planned services
Realtime transitRoute, Matrix and Reach; supplied or polled, with Service Alerts
Supplied trafficDrive Route and Matrix
CompareReach surfaces
Monte CarloScheduled depart-at transit Route, Matrix and Reach


The engine does not combine planned branch edits into schedules or optimize fares. Prepare those inputs with the compiler or Studio.


Platform and build records


Release archives are built and tested for Linux x64 and ARM64 (glibc 2.39 or newer, built on Ubuntu 24.04), macOS ARM64 and Windows x64. For an older Linux, build from source on that system. manifest.json records the target, source commit, uncommitted-change flag, source digest and file hashes; a dirty: true package is a development build. Keep the manifest with a deployment. The verification record lists the checks a release passes.


Run the checks


From a source checkout:


Shell
cargo test --manifest-path crates/vigo-runtime/Cargo.toml \
  --no-default-features --features standalone
cargo clippy --manifest-path crates/vigo-runtime/Cargo.toml \
  --no-default-features --features standalone --all-targets -- -D warnings
VIGO_STANDALONE_PATH=/absolute/path/to/vigo npm run check:standalone
python3 test/check-standalone-package.py /absolute/path/to/package.tar.gz
npm run docs:standalone
npm run check:standalone-docs


The documentation check builds the fixture City, runs every request on this page against the engine, compares the response excerpts, checks that every command-line flag, request field and environment variable is documented, and serves the guide over HTTP. Passing checks establish the tested model, not field accuracy, station accessibility or deployment capacity.

How VIGO works
How VIGO computes answers
7 min readSource
On this page
TransitThe timetableThe searchTransfersWalking to and from transitRealtimeSeveral journeysWalkingDrivingBicycleReachMonte CarloExactness and its boundariesHow the algorithms are verified
VIGO answers each question with an exact search over a declared model: the prepared timetable, the directed street graphs and the request's rules. "Exact" means the returned time is optimal for that model, not that the model matches the real world. This page explains the model and the searches, and marks where VIGO bounds, samples or estimates instead.


Every runtime uses the same Rust kernels. The engine, the compiler, Studio and Python differ in how they are called, not in how they route.


Transit


The timetable


A City's timetable is a list of connections: one vehicle moving from one stop to the next, with a departure and an arrival time, its trip, and whether boarding and alighting are allowed. For a service date, VIGO activates the trips whose calendars and exceptions run that day, plus trips from adjacent days that overlap the search. Times are seconds on the service day, so a trip at 25:10 stays on the day it was published.


GTFS frequencies become ordinary connections. exact_times=1 windows are expanded when the City is built; exact_times=0 templates are read as a departure at the start of each window and then every headway, before the window's exclusive end. Because GTFS gives no exact times for the second kind, those departures are scheduled estimates and the City records the limitation frequency_based_service.


Explicit in-seat links (transfer_type=4) and consecutive same-terminal trips on one block become through-runs: the rider stays aboard and the change counts as one boarding.


The search


Transit uses one connection scan for every City and every request size. Connections are scanned in departure order, and each stop keeps its earliest arrival; a connection can be used when the rider is at its stop in time, or already aboard its trip. Arrive-by runs the same scan backward from the deadline.


QuestionObjective, in order
Depart-atEarliest arrival, then fewer boardings, then less walking
Arrive-byLatest departure; among those, fewer boardings, less walking, then earlier arrival


A transfer cap (maxTransfers) constrains the search itself, by tracking the best arrival for each number of boardings, so a slower route is found when the fastest needs too many changes. A Matrix shares one forward scan per distinct origin, or one reverse scan per distinct destination; every requested cell is still answered.


Transfers


Transfer permissions are prepared into the timetable before the scan. No query keeps per-trip transfer state.


  • Physical transfers. Preparation finds the walking connections between stops: directed OSM paths up to 500 m, declared GTFS pathways, and station membership. A rule cannot restore a connection removed by allowStreetTransfers: false or the wheelchair profile.
  • Stop-level GTFS rules. transfers.txt rows without route or trip selectors apply at their stops, expanded through parent stations; a platform's own rule overrides the one it inherits. transfer_type=3 forbids the transfer; transfer_type=2 sets the minimum time; recommended and timed rules set no minimum, and the guarantee of a timed transfer is not represented.
  • Minimum walking time. Each transfer takes at least the published minimum and at least its distance at walking speed.
  • Station fallback. Platforms of one parent station with no rule or declared pathway use at least 120 seconds, or their distance at walking speed, reported as parent_station_fallback.
  • The request. minimumTransferBufferMinutes is added after walking and the published minimum. It never delays the first boarding, the final walk or staying aboard.


Route- and trip-scoped transfer selectors are kept in the City's transfer_rules table but are not applied: the stop-level rule governs. Flex interchanges still resolve the most specific rule for their conditional legs.


Walking to and from transit


Each origin and destination searches the directed pedestrian graph for stops within maxWalkKm. The walking time includes the City's access padding and any station pathway. A direct walk is computed separately and wins when it arrives sooner, unless requireTransitRide is set.


Realtime


A realtime request compiles its Trip Updates into a separate timetable: matched trips get their predicted times, canceled trips lose their connections, and unreported trips keep their schedule. The same scan then runs on that timetable. Realtime is a different input, not a different algorithm.


Several journeys


Alternatives, journey windows and shared legs build on the exact search but are bounded:


FeatureWhat is exactWhat is bounded
AlternativesEach returned journey is feasible and correctly timedThe candidate set is limited by count, arrival slack and a label budget
Journey windowsEach sampled minute is answered exactlyOnly whole-minute samples; not a continuous profile
Via pointsEach segment is exact for its start timeUp to eight partial journeys per point; not every itinerary
Shared legsEach option is a complete, feasible journeyOne leg changed at a time, within 30 minutes and fixed counts
FlexThe returned journey is feasibleCan be up to 60 seconds later than the best conditional journey


Walking


The pedestrian graph is built from OSM ways with pedestrian permission, in both directions unless a way says otherwise. Explicit foot=no, private access, foot=use_sidepath, impassable barriers and unresolved conditions are excluded; a motor-vehicle one-way restriction alone does not restrict walking. Walking evidence describes the rules and station costs in detail.


Paths use a customizable contraction hierarchy (CCH): a prepared index that answers shortest-path queries exactly and quickly. The hierarchy is built once per City and never removes streets or changes their lengths.


A free coordinate attaches to its nearest vertex or two-way edge; the short straight connector is part of the cost and is reported as unverified. VIGO never draws a straight line where a street path is missing.


Driving


Drive uses a directed road graph from OSM with free-flow speeds by road class and maximum speed. Its hierarchy is built with the City and persisted. A supplied traffic snapshot customizes the hierarchy's weights for one request: a fixed set of costs, never faster than free flow, and not a forecast that changes during the trip. Turn penalties, signals and intersection delays are not modeled.


A free coordinate attaches to the nearest drivable road and enters it mid-segment in its own direction; the gap is a walk.


Bicycle


Bike uses a directed graph with bicycle access, contraflow, surfaces, mapped incline, dismount sections and turn restrictions, including restrictions through intermediate ways. Its hierarchy keeps the incoming road in every state, so turn restrictions are exact.


  • Preference and time are separate. The profile (balanced, quiet or fast) and traffic-stress limit choose the route by a preference cost. The reported duration is the physical travel time at the chosen speed, adjusted for surface and incline.
  • Time-dependent rules. With a date and a known timezone, access, one-way directions, dismount periods and turn restrictions are evaluated when the bicycle enters each segment, and the search can wait for a road or turn to open. A segment entered while open can be finished. An arrive-by route is anchored at the deadline and replayed forward to check every movement; it is proved optimal when no move must wait, and otherwise searched backward through the hierarchy.
  • Many-to-many. Matrix and Reach share rank sweeps across endpoints, and check each witness's distance and time before reporting it.
  • Stress. Traffic stress (LTS 1–4) is estimated from road class, speed and lanes, after Conveyal's published labeler; OSM lts tags take precedence.


The bicycle hierarchy can keep part of its structure in the user cache, bound to the City's source; opening rebuilds the rest exactly. The cache holds graph data only.


Reach


Transit Reach runs the connection scan once from the origin (or backward from the destination), then spreads walking from every reached stop and from the origin itself over the directed streets, within the walking budget and the largest cutoff. The result is the earliest time at every reached part of every street.


The raster is drawn from that result:


  • Street sampling (default) gives each cell the least time on the reached streets inside it. Cells with no reached street stay empty, and a filled cell does not prove a route to its center.
  • Cell-center sampling routes to the center of every cell with the Matrix rules.


Areas are polygons around reachable cells, with holes and islands kept; contours interpolate the raster at each cutoff. Both depend on the grid's resolution. Drive and Bike Reach route to every cell center.


Arrive-by Reach reverses the whole process: the timetable is scanned backward, and walking runs backward over directed streets so one-way paths keep their direction.


Monte Carlo


A Monte Carlo request repeats a query at every minute of a departure window. Planned frequency services without exact times receive a random phase per sample, shared by every stop and endpoint in that sample. VIGO reports nearest-rank percentiles that include unreachable samples as infinitely long. It assumes on-time operation and riders who know the timetable. See Monte Carlo routing and accessibility.


Exactness and its boundaries


ClaimHolds when
A transit time is optimalFor the prepared timetable, transfer rules, walking policy and request limits
A street path is shortestFor the prepared graph, its permissions and the attachment of each endpoint
A blocked answer means no journeyUnder the request's date, horizon, walking limit and transfer cap, within the City's coverage
A Matrix cell equals the RouteFor the same endpoints and settings; ties can choose a different equally good journey
Two runtimes agreeFor the same City, request and version


VIGO does not establish:


  • that the timetable or map matches reality, or that a station path, entrance or crossing exists beyond what the data declares;
  • delays, crowding, missed connections or reliability, beyond supplied realtime predictions;
  • turn penalties or intersection delays for driving;
  • opportunities, demand or welfare: Reach is travel time, not accessibility.


How the algorithms are verified


Public tests compare VIGO with independent reference implementations that never supply production answers: Floyd–Warshall shortest paths for walking and driving, whole-trip enumeration from raw GTFS for transit, and every stop-to-stop pair at each boarding boundary. A permanent fixture checks that new Cities stay readable by the published reference runtime. See Checking routing accuracy to run them and to validate your own City.

How VIGO works
Walking costs and source evidence
4 min readSource
On this page
Time and connectivity are separatePedestrian permissionsWhat a returned route establishesRebuild to apply these rules
This page explains how VIGO prices walks between streets, stops and platforms, which OSM permissions it follows, and what a returned walk does and does not establish. Every runtime uses the same prepared City data and rules.


Time and connectivity are separate


A GTFS transfer minimum constrains the time between services. It does not describe a physical path or permit arbitrarily fast walking. Before searching, VIGO prices each expanded stop pair at the larger of the published minimum and its distance divided by the configured walking speed, rounded up to a whole second. The distance is at least the straight-line separation of valid stop coordinates. That separation supplies a lower bound; a missing interior path remains unknown.


GTFS pathways describe directed station connections. An explicit traversal_time remains a source cost, including for lifts and moving walkways. If it is absent, VIGO derives a time from the available length and walking policy. A declared pathway supports the feed's connectivity model; it is not a current field measurement. When a station declares pathways and public entrances, coordinate access uses those entrances; snapping straight to a platform cannot bypass the station connections.


The walking floor enters preparation before boarding selection, so a depart-at query may choose a later connection and an arrive-by query may require an earlier departure. Route and both scalar and journey Matrix modes use those same costs.


Pedestrian permissions


The OSM importer reads tags on ways and their nodes, including packed dense nodes. It excludes foot=no, foot=private, and foot=use_sidepath, honors explicit pedestrian permission over generic access, and preserves directed pedestrian rules. A motor-vehicle one-way restriction alone does not prohibit walking in the reverse direction.


An explicit pedestrian permission also overrides general conditional restrictions, and a conditional rule that only permits walking where the base rule already permits it does not disconnect the way. Restrictive or unknown pedestrian conditions, opening hours and conditional directions stay excluded, because VIGO does not evaluate them at journey time.


For nodes, impassable barriers and denied access exclude incident pedestrian segments. Ambiguous gates require explicit permission. Foot/access conditional rules and opening hours other than 24/7 are excluded because this static model does not evaluate their conditions. This conservative policy can reduce coverage, including approaches to a blocked barrier. Driving retains its separate permissions. See the OSM definitions of foot access and pedestrian direction.


What a returned route establishes


Closed elevator ways describe cabin footprints, so they are not imported as horizontal walking loops. Open inclined-elevator ways retain their existing walking treatment. Station vertical travel still requires declared pathways; removing a cabin outline does not invent a street-to-platform connection.


streetPathVerified concerns the prepared street graph; it is not independent proof of an entire door-to-platform walk. Free-coordinate snapping is returned separately as endpointConnector, with streetPathVerified: false. The walk's line still starts or ends at the requested coordinate, so a journey is drawn without gaps; its first or last segment is that connector. An assumed station interior has stationAccessStatus: "unverified"; a published transfer minimum does not change that status. Selected station costs and stop chains are exposed in accessCost when available.


An independent physical audit needs a continuous, directed source path, legal node/way access, and evidence for the links between the requested location, street, stop, entrance, and platform. A line near an OSM street is insufficient. Source gaps require better mapped entrances, agency pathways, or validated access links. Even complete source evidence does not establish current closures or observed travel times.


An interior GTFS node may omit coordinates. VIGO retains its declared pathway connections and stop ID but omits that node from displayed geometry, setting stationGeometryStatus: "incomplete". A line between the remaining known coordinates is schematic. If a source-timed pathway also lacks length and located endpoints, its distance contributes only a zero lower bound and the leg reports stationDistanceStatus: "lower_bound"; it is not measured zero-distance walking. When traversal_time is absent, stairs with a nonzero stair_count use one second per step and fare/exit gates use five seconds. These fixed routing assumptions are recorded as gtfs_pathway_estimated, retain stationAccessStatus: "unverified", and are floored by available distance at the configured walking pace. They are not measured or agency-published traversal times. Explicit traversal times take precedence. Other pathways without time, length, or distinct located endpoints remain excluded and reported as unpriced_pathways. The declared station topology remains in force, so exclusion cannot create a fallback shortcut. A feed-supplied connection alone does not certify its physical duration.


Rebuild to apply these rules


These rules are prepared into a City when it is built. To apply them to older data, build a new City from the original GTFS and OSM into a new directory, and keep the old City with its original runtime for reproducibility. The engine rejects prepared data whose street, timetable or transfer policy is older than it supports.


Prepared layerCurrent versionWhat it adds
Street storeSchema v6Node restrictions from the PBF; platform outlines excluded from walking
Routing storeSchema v3Missing coordinates and pathway costs distinguished from real zeros
Transfer semanticsv4Pathway modes and stair counts kept from the GTFS
Prepared access policyv9Street transfers through public entrances and directed station pathways


Each transfer between boardings uses at most one external transfer edge, and the itinerary keeps every original pathway segment. Declared pathways suppress invented parent-station shortcuts.


The public regression checks use generated inputs:


Shell
npm run check:osm-pbf
npm run check:national-focused
npm run check:standalone


These checks exercise node barriers, access overrides, malformed node tags, pedestrian direction, physically feasible transfer selection in both time directions, scalar/journey matrices, and rejection of old prepared data. They test the implementation and declared input model, not the completeness of any agency's pedestrian map.

How VIGO works
GTFS support matrix
10 min readSource
On this page
Explicit linked tripsRealtime replacement tripsSemantic coverage written to store metadataRequired fixture policy
This matrix is the public boundary of what VIGO's routing uses from GTFS. "Imported" alone is not support: the routing column says whether a feature changes which journeys are feasible. Every import records a feature inventory.


Pickup and drop-off permissions are compiled per connection: a forbidden boarding is absent from the departure index, a forbidden alighting cannot end a ride, and a passenger already aboard stays on through either kind of restricted stop. Transfers are prepared into one stop-level transfer graph before the scan; see How VIGO computes answers. When a feed uses features VIGO does not support, the rest is routed as a supported_scheduled_core, with the exclusions attached to every Result. Only multiple agency timezones block a whole feed.


GTFS feature or caseImportRouting behaviorClassification
calendar.txt onlyYesWeekly service within start/end dates.Supported.
calendar_dates.txt onlyYesType 1 adds and type 2 removes service on the exact date.Supported.
Calendar plus exceptionsYesExceptions override the weekly calendar for the date.Supported.
Missing both calendar tablesRejectedNo service date can be established.Rejected malformed input.
Times greater than 24 hoursYesPreserved as seconds on the originating service day.Supported within the query horizon.
Trips crossing midnightYesConnections retain their originating service date. Native clock-date requests load active adjacent service days, including overnight headway windows.Supported within the service-day range and query horizon.
Trips extending across more than one midnightParsedSame coordinate model; default horizon may exclude them and the public CLI clock is bounded.Bounded; caller must set a sufficient horizon and service-day coordinate.
Invalid minute or second fieldsRejectedValues such as 08:60:00 or 08:00:60 do not normalize silently.Rejected malformed input.
Agency timezone, one timezoneInventoriedNative service epochs use local noon minus twelve elapsed hours; realtime instants use the same timezone.Calendar, overnight and DST regression checks cover the native APIs.
Multiple agency timezones in one storeInventoriedExact routing is blocked.Unsupported and visible.
frequencies.txt, exact_times=1Yes, boundedThe template trip is expanded into deterministic fixed departures for each declared frequency window. Generated instances retain route, service, permissions, and shape identity.Supported for bounded deterministic windows.
frequencies.txt, exact_times=0YesThe template departs at each window's start and then every headway, before the exclusive end_time, as ordinary trips.Supported as scheduled estimates; limitation frequency_based_service.
Overlapping or mixed frequency windowsRejectedImport requires nonoverlapping windows and a single exact_times value per trip.Invalid feed rejected before publication.
Shapes presentYesOrdered trip stops are matched to a monotone shape slice.Supported for rendering; feasibility never depends on shape.
Shapes missing or unusableYesTimetable route remains valid. Ordinary network lenses show no inferred route alignment; selected-itinerary and Shape/Risk QA views may show a dashed, explicitly inferred stop sequence.Timetable supported; published ride geometry unavailable.
Duplicate stop namesYesIdentity is stop_id, not name.Supported.
Parent stations and platformsYesExplicit parent transfer rules expand to child service platforms; selected stations expand to service members. Without an explicit rule, service members share a modeled 120-second connection, reported as parent_station_fallback with schematic geometry.Supported for location_type 0/1; fallback time is not a measured station pathway.
Deeper location_type hierarchyPreparedStation membership includes descendants. Boarding areas connect to their parent platform for boarding/alighting; a platform cannot create an unproved shortcut between its areas.Pathway-based access supported; unlocated boarding areas cannot be selected directly.
pathways.txt direction and traversal timeYesCreates directed transfer edges; explicit traversal times take precedence. Stairs with a stair count and fare/exit gates receive labeled estimated costs when time is omitted. Bidirectional rows create the reverse edge. Parallel pathways use the lowest available traversal cost; unpriced paths without enough data remain excluded.Supported within the prepared pathway graph.
Pathway wheelchair/slope/width attributesProfile dependentApplied during build --wheelchair; ordinary Cities inventory them without filtering.See Wheelchair routing.
Transfer type 0YesDirected recommended transfer using declared/default duration.Supported within transfer model.
Transfer type 1 timed transferYesA stop-level rule with no minimum time. The guarantee, holding a vehicle for a late connection, is not represented.Supported without the guarantee; limitation timed_transfer_guarantee.
Transfer type 2 minimum timeYesDeclared minimum traversal time is enforced.Supported.
Transfer type 3 forbiddenYesDirected pair, including expanded parent/platform pairs, is forbidden and cannot be regenerated by proximity. A same-stop prohibition blocks reboarding after a ride while preserving an origin's initial boarding.Supported with permanent SQLite, compact-kernel, and matrix regressions.
Transfer type 4/5 in-seat semanticsRetained in optional trip_linksRust compiles explicit type 4 links, including different terminal stops, into through runs; type 5 never grants a continuation. Source trip identities and dwell remain visible.Route, Matrix and Reach count one boarding; onboard movement and dwell are riding time.
Route- or trip-scoped transfer selectorsNot appliedRetained in transfer_rules; the stop-level rule governs the transfer. Stop-level rules use parent-station expansion and GTFS specificity: a platform's own rule overrides its station's.Stop-level semantics only; Flex interchanges still resolve scoped selectors.
Nearby stops without explicit transferPreparedOne native multi-target street search creates every directed OSM-reachable alight-to-board edge within 500 m. Each edge stores its routed distance; unproved radial pairs remain visible counts.Supported within the City street model.
pickup_type=1 / drop_off_type=1YesThe complete scheduled trip is retained. Boarding is prohibited only at a stop with pickup_type=1; alighting is prohibited only at a stop with drop_off_type=1; through-riding remains legal.Supported for fixed-stop routing.
pickup_type / drop_off_type value 2Conditionalflex: {} includes journeys through timed fixed stops with booking requirements; ordinary routing excludes those events and keeps through-riding.No booking or availability confirmation; see GTFS Flex.
pickup_type / drop_off_type value 3YesFixed flag stops permit boarding/alighting, assuming the rider signals or notifies the driver. This does not enable continuous stopping or advance-booking service.Visible driver_coordinated_stops condition. Rebuild Cities imported before this fix: compiled permission bits cannot distinguish flag stops from prohibited events.
Continuous pickup/drop-offConditionalWith flex: {}, boarding and alighting follow directed GTFS shapes and stop-time permission overrides. Intermediate times are interpolated and labeled as estimates.Booking and driver-coordination requirements remain visible; ordinary fixed-stop routing is unchanged.
GTFS Flex zones, location groups and booking rulesYesWith flex: {}, conditional rides join fixed service in one search.See GTFS Flex.
Loop routesYesSequence, not stop identity, orders a trip; reconstruction can retain repeated locations.Supported, with adversarial regression coverage required.
Repeated stop in one tripYesDistinct stop_sequence events remain distinct.Supported.
block_id interliningPartialConsecutive same-terminal trips with a shared block, service ID and service day use Rust through-runs; explicit links take precedence.Other block models require explicit links.
Duplicate stop, route, trip, or calendar IDsRejectedA primary-key conflict aborts the temporary build; no partial store is published.Rejected malformed input with adversarial atomicity coverage.
Missing shape ID referenced by a tripYesTimetable routing remains available, but published alignment is unavailable; any selected/QA stop-sequence line is dashed and marked inferred.Timetable supported; published ride geometry unavailable.
Untimed interior stop-time gapsYesTimed endpoints remain connected and the itinerary reports interpolated-stop-time-gap; no exact timestamp is claimed for omitted interior events.Supported with degraded timing precision.
Malformed required tableRejectedBuild does not commit the temporary store.Supported rejection.
Broken core referencesRejectedUnknown trip routes/services, parent stations, transfer endpoints, frequency trips, and stop-time trip/stop references abort the temporary build. Missing shapes remain a supported timetable-only case as declared above.Rejected malformed input with adversarial atomicity coverage.


Explicit linked trips


The optional trip_links SQLite table preserves from_trip_id, to_trip_id, and transfer_type (4 or 5), including feed namespaces. Existing Cities without it remain readable. A City whose importer discarded these rows must be rebuilt from the original GTFS; no runtime can recover the missing evidence.


The Rust runtime compiles active, chronological type 4 chains once per timetable view, after realtime updates. Splitting and coupling produce bounded through paths. Original trips remain available for partial journeys and for reconstructing source trip IDs, shapes, headsigns and service dates. No new search algorithm or JavaScript routing path is introduced. Ordinary Cities have no extra connection arrays; linked paths add only their own connections. Limits (512 trips per path, 200,000 paths, and four times the original segment count with a 100,000-segment floor) fail explicitly rather than truncate results. Path retention is also capped at one million trip references. Before copying columns, an estimate including spare vector capacity, physical-part copies and name tables must fit one eighth of detected memory capacity, capped at 128 MiB. This bounds estimated additional allocations; it is not a process RSS guarantee.


A public transit leg following an in-seat continuation has continuation: { "type": "stay_aboard", "durationSeconds": 300 }, for example. The duration is the actual onboard gap before that leg, including zero; it is part of journey riding time, not waiting for another vehicle. Transfer limits apply to boardings, not the number of displayed source-trip legs. Boarding or alighting restrictions at the boundary do not force passengers off the vehicle. Through-journey fares remain unavailable where the fare catalog cannot describe the corresponding fare-leg joins; VIGO does not invent an additional or free fare.


Explicit links may connect different terminal stops: the interval between the first trip's arrival and the next trip's departure is onboard movement or dwell. It is included in riding time, without inventing a passenger walking leg. Overlapping clocks, canceled/truncated endpoints and inactive trips do not establish continuity.


The optional trip_operations table retains block identifiers and bicycle permissions. Rust infers consecutive same-terminal block continuations only within one service ID and service day. Adjacency comes from the original schedule, so cancellation cannot skip over a missing middle trip. Explicit links (including type 5) take precedence. Different-terminal blocks and blocks spanning different service IDs still need explicit links. Old Cities without these optional tables retain their existing behavior.


node test/check-linked-trips.mjs checks raw-GTFS import, forward/reverse Route, Matrix, Reach, source identities, dwell, boarding restrictions, realtime, branching and scenario exclusions. The native unit tests cover service-day boundaries and invalid continuity.


Realtime replacement trips


GTFS Realtime REPLACEMENT (experimental, enum value 5) replaces a known trip's complete stop sequence in Rust. Every call must identify an unambiguous existing City stop and an increasing stop sequence, with absolute arrival/departure clocks at every call. Changed intermediate stops and realtime pickup/drop-off restrictions are supported. Incomplete, backwards or unknown-stop replacements are rejected and reported in realtime diagnostics. NEW and DUPLICATED still need new trip identity construction and are not supported by this replacement path.


Semantic coverage written to store metadata


blockingRoutingFeatures has one code for otherwise importable GTFS: multiple_agency_timezones. A City with it cannot route.


Nonblocking routingLimitations keep the City routable in supported_scheduled_core mode. Each records a count and a detail, and an exactness of approximate or unsupported:


CodeMeaning
frequency_based_serviceexact_times=0 templates, routed as departures every headway from each window's start
repaired_trip_timesBackward times repaired by delaying events at most 600 seconds
backward_trip_timesTrips needing larger corrections, excluded whole
on_demand_boarding_or_alighting, driver_coordinated_stops, restricted_boarding_or_alighting, continuous_pickup_or_drop_offPickup and drop-off types that need booking, coordination or Flex
scoped_transfer_rulesRoute- or trip-scoped transfer rules, kept but not applied
timed_transfer_guaranteetransfer_type=1 rows; the guarantee to hold a vehicle is not represented
in_seat_transfer_rules, block_interliningContinuations VIGO cannot represent exactly
pathway_accessibility, unpriced_pathways, station_entrances, station_level_hierarchyStation data the walking graph cannot fully use
wheelchair_accessibility, bicycle_accessibilityTrip and stop accessibility attributes outside the active profile
feature_inventory_incompleteThe import could not inventory every feature


"Nonblocking" does not mean full-feed support: it means VIGO makes a narrower, explicit claim over the compiled scheduled core instead of disabling unrelated service. A journey in this mode is optimal over that core, and no_path means no path exists in the core; an excluded trip or rule could still change full-feed reachability. Holding a vehicle after its scheduled departure is not predicted.


Public comparisons require matching assumptionsFingerprint values. Scenario and observation content are interventions excluded from that fingerprint; route constraints, City revision and engine version are included. Equivalent requests with omitted and explicit defaults are treated as different until normalized.


Required fixture policy


Each row classified supported must have a miniature feed that would fail if the field were merely parsed. Each visible unsupported row must have a fixture that imports successfully and records the feature code. Permission fixtures must prove that the trip remains connected, illegal boarding and alighting events are rejected, and through-riding remains legal in the resident kernel, shared matrix path, and merged stores. Quarantined transfer fixtures must prove that the unsupported row is absent from the generic graph. Multiple-timezone fixtures must still prove a feed-wide blocked result. Rebuild an older SQLite store before using it for a published result.

How VIGO works
Checking routing accuracy
4 min readSource
On this page
Reproducible independent checksDeclare the model before comparing answersChecks required for a real CityWhat passing means
VIGO uses one exact Transit Matrix search for every City and OD set. City names, endpoint distance, and matrix dimensions do not select different algorithms. Independent reference implementations live in tests and never supply production answers.


Accuracy has two parts: the search must solve the declared model, and the model must faithfully represent the input data and the intended trip. A fast result or agreement between two VIGO interfaces establishes neither part by itself.


Reproducible independent checks


Shell
npm run build:rust-routing-kernel
npm run check:accuracy
# Extend the same checks to 100 deterministic generated networks:
VIGO_ACCURACY_SEEDS=100 npm run check:accuracy


test/check-routing-accuracy.mjs generates its own public synthetic inputs. A failing run retains the input directory and reports its seed and query. It uses:


  • Floyd–Warshall, implemented independently from VIGO's routing and contraction code, to check every directed walking distance and driving travel time on weighted graphs. Alternating graphs allow only forward edges, so unreachable OD pairs are checked as well. Drive witnesses are checked edge by edge against the input weights.
  • Whole-trip enumeration from generated raw GTFS, independently of VIGO's compiled connection scan, to check earliest arrival and latest departure. The fixtures exercise pickup/drop-off restrictions, staying aboard restricted stops, dwell, midnight, inactive dates, missed connections, published same-stop minimums and forbidden transfers. Zero-duration trips are deliberately placed in reverse dependency order; all scans resolve same-time connections to a fixed point.
  • Every stop-to-stop OD at each boarding-time boundary on the generated transit networks. This covers each distinct exact-stop departure interval in those fixtures. Separate queries check Matrix permutations, duplicate endpoints, scalar Route parity and materialized ride times and permissions.


Separate raw GTFS fixtures verify 0-, 30-, 90- and 300-second platform transfer rules, parent-station expansion, and forbidden transfers through Route, Matrix and arrive-by queries.


The normal suite runs eight seeds on every supported CI operating system. Larger runs use the same algorithms and assertions. They do not select easier queries based on a City's identity or on previous outcomes.


Declare the model before comparing answers


The engine adds no implicit boarding buffer. Same-stop vehicle changes honor published GTFS minimum transfer times and forbidden transfers; staying aboard does not incur a transfer minimum. The minimum affects boarding readiness, not the alighting time or final egress. Explicit transfer edges retain their durations without an added boarding margin or a 60-second floor. Native diagnostics report transferBoardSlackSeconds: 0. A published platform-to-platform transfer rule takes precedence over the station walking fallback.


GTFS service dates, after-midnight times, pickup/drop-off permissions and transfer rules must come from the same input snapshot. Their definitions are in the GTFS Schedule Reference.


Record the exact date, time zone, departure/arrival objective, walking speed, per-endpoint walking limit, direct-walk limit, transfer policy, search horizon and live-state snapshot. Distinguish exact selected stops from arbitrary coordinates. Coordinate snapping and street access are part of the query model and require their own verification.


Checks required for a real City


  1. Validate compilation. Check raw GTFS references, calendars, exceptions, permissions and transferred identities against the compiled City. Inspect omitted or unsupported features. Check directed OSM access and connectivity, including isolated components, bridges and one-way streets.
  2. Verify journey witnesses. Each ride must reference an active raw trip, follow its stop order, use legal boarding/alighting events and preserve published times. Every street segment must follow allowed directed edges. Check endpoint connectors separately so a correct graph path cannot conceal an invalid snap.
  3. Compare independently. Run the same inputs and query policies through an independent router such as OpenTripPlanner. Its route-request documentation describes configurable routing policies. Retain both itineraries and investigate each disagreement; matching durations alone is insufficient, and another engine's answer is not ground truth.
  4. Test changes that should preserve or constrain the answer. Rename IDs, reorder input rows and Matrix endpoints, move the complete City directory, and repeat after unrelated queries. Answers should remain stable. Under identical horizons and policies, removing service must not improve earliest arrival, and adding service must not make it worse.
  5. Retain failures. Keep false reachable results, false blocked results, invalid witnesses, timing discrepancies, setup failures and query errors as separate outcomes. Save the smallest reproducing input and add a regression before accepting a fix. Do not change the oracle to match an unexplained engine answer.


For exact graph and timetable comparisons, require zero feasibility disagreements. Use only the documented public timestamp rounding tolerance when comparing numeric results. Equivalent optimal itineraries may differ in geometry or route choice; validate feasibility and the objective before comparing presentation details.


What passing means


The independent suite validates the generated graph and timetable models under their declared policy. It does not establish correct coordinate snapping on arbitrary OSM extracts, complete GTFS transfer-rule support, live-provider correctness, or real delivered travel times. Those require retained City-specific input and witness checks. A universal algorithmic guarantee comes from the algorithm's invariants and input assumptions; finite testing supports it but cannot prove every possible City or OD.

How VIGO works
Known limits
3 min readSource
On this page
GTFSTransit Route and MatrixStreetsRealtimeCity reuse and platformsScenarios and Reach
VIGO models the City revision and query it is given. It does not certify real-world service, demand, safety or operations. How VIGO computes answers separates what is exact from what is bounded or estimated.


GTFS


  • VIGO uses the GTFS features listed in GTFS support. Unsupported or malformed features are reported during the build.
  • Frequency templates with exact_times=0 are read as a departure at the start of each window and then every headway. GTFS gives no exact times for them, so these are scheduled estimates.
  • Route- and trip-scoped transfer rules are kept but not applied; the stop-level rule governs those transfers. Timed-transfer guarantees are not represented.
  • Missing shapes do not prevent routing but limit map geometry.
  • Explicit GTFS in-seat links keep passengers aboard across trip changes and count one boarding. Block-based continuation is inferred only for consecutive same-terminal trips on one block, service and day; other continuations need explicit links.
  • Staying aboard must move the rider onward. A journey boards a looping vehicle at its last pass, and alternatives that stay aboard through a turnaround only to return to a stop the rider could already reach are dropped.


Transit Route and Matrix


  • Arrive-by Matrix durations include any wait between arrival and the deadline; use journeys for the actual arrival.
  • Time reserves change route choice, but VIGO computes no arrival probabilities.
  • A finite maxTransfers cap cannot be combined with transit via points.
  • Returning to a station already visited can be valid in the timetable; it is flagged, not excluded.
  • Without an explicit rule or declared pathways, platforms of one parent station use a transfer time of at least 120 seconds, or their distance at walking speed. These legs report transferSource: "parent_station_fallback" and a schematic line.
  • A street route to a platform coordinate does not establish an entrance-to-platform connection. Walks touching subway platforms report stationAccessStatus: "unverified" unless a declared pathway covers them. Untimed stairs and gates use explicit estimates (one second per step, five seconds per gate). Scalar Matrix results do not carry this per-leg evidence.
  • Departure windows sample whole minutes; they are not continuous profiles.


Streets


  • Walk, Drive and Bike depend on OSM coverage and directions.
  • Pedestrian attachment searches vertices within 160 m and edges within 80 m. A missing attachment is not proof that no path exists.
  • Platform polygons describe an area, not a path; routing across their interiors is not modeled.
  • A free coordinate keeps its nearest attachment even when that street connects poorly, such as a ramp or bridge above the point. Attaching to several streets would let a connector cross barriers. Place points on the street or path the traveler will use.
  • Authorized endpoint access is an opt-in assumption; it does not establish permissions, gate hours or missing links.
  • Drive does not model every turn restriction, signal or intersection delay, and traffic must be supplied.


Realtime


  • Realtime transit needs explicit realtime selection and a snapshot, supplied or polled. It applies to Route in every runtime and to transit Matrix and Reach only in the engine. Vehicle Positions never change routing. In the engine, a fresh NO_SERVICE Service Alert closes what it selects; other alerts are reported on legs.
  • Only FULL_DATASET feeds are decoded. Added, duplicated and unscheduled trips are unsupported for routing.
  • Feed and record timestamps must be at most 180 seconds old and 60 seconds ahead. Missing timestamps do not establish freshness.


City reuse and platforms


  • Copy the entire City directory. Executables are specific to an operating system and CPU; City data is portable across the supported 64-bit platforms.
  • Older Cities without a persisted driving hierarchy rebuild it when a process opens them; rebuilding the City from source persists it.
  • A new active-service pattern, a changed walking policy or an evicted timetable needs preparation. Missing or corrupt required street files are errors.
  • Studio's settings, drafts and live connections are local and do not travel inside a City. Studio cannot open compiler City directories in this release.


Scenarios and Reach


  • Planned service changes apply to transit Reach, and in the engine and Studio to transit Route. Traffic applies to Drive Route and Matrix. Drive Reach uses free-flow speeds without traffic or scenarios.
  • maxTransfers limits changes in baseline and scenario Reach; walking never counts as a boarding.
  • Reach rasterizes reached streets while Matrix evaluates coordinates, so their cells can differ under matching settings.
  • Reach measures modeled travel time, not people, jobs, demand, welfare, behavior or operational feasibility.

VIGO Python
VIGO Python 1.0.01 min readSource
On this page
Start with a working exampleThree questions, one CityRead the result correctlyKeep repeated work efficientReference and support
VIGO Python 1.0.0 gives scripts and notebooks a small set of objects for transport analysis. Build or open a City, run Route, Matrix, or Reach, and retain the Result. Reuse one open City for repeated work.


Start with a working example


  • Your first queryInstall the package, select Engine 1.0, and route using a prepared City.
  • Build a CityTurn local GTFS and OSM inputs into a reusable network.
  • Calculate a matrixEvaluate many origins and destinations together, with optional journeys.
  • Compare a service changeRun baseline and Scenario queries on the same City.


Three questions, one City


Python
import vigo

with vigo.open("./boston") as city:
    result = city.route(
        [-71.11902, 42.37334],
        [-71.05524, 42.35227],
        depart_at="08:00",
        service_date="2026-10-05",
    )
    if result.status == "ready":
        print(result.duration_minutes)


This example requires a City covering central Boston and a feed active on the chosen date. Coordinates are [longitude, latitude]. Transit may choose a direct walk; set require_transit_ride=True when a boarding is required.


QueryAnswerReference
RouteA journey between ordered placesRoute
MatrixTravel times for pairs of placesMatrix
ReachReachable streets and areas within a time budgetReach


Read the result correctly


Python uses ready and blocked Result statuses. Ordinary queries use minute-valued travel times; opt-in Monte Carlo distributions retain seconds. A completed Matrix can contain blocked rows. Invalid inputs and execution failures raise exceptions. Results and exports explains each field and the comparison rules.


The public Engine CLI and HTTP schemas use seconds and different status names. Use Python's documented Result properties in Python applications.


Keep repeated work efficient


Use a context manager, retain the open City, and request Matrix journeys or geometry only when needed. Install the optional speed extra for accelerated response decoding. Use result.iter_rows() to copy only consumed rows. Runtime and performance explains process reuse, timing, and resource lifetime.


Reference and support

Your first Python query
VIGO Python 1.0.03 min readSource
On this page
1. Install2. Prepare the City3. Run a journey query4. Read and reuse the answer
Install VIGO Python 1.0.0, select Engine 1.0, and open a prepared City. The example below asks for a journey from Harvard Square to South Station.


1. Install


For a packaged installation, download the VIGO-Python-… ZIP matching your OS and CPU from the VIGO releases page and unzip it. It contains the wheel, INSTALL.txt, and the runtime manifest. Replace the filename below with the unzipped wheel:


Shell
python -m pip install "/path/to/vigo-1.0.0-py3-none-PLATFORM.whl[speed]"


Platform wheels include Node, the headless CLI bundle, the Rust kernel, and the vigo engine executable. The optional speed extra adds accelerated JSON decoding. Omit the extra for the dependency-free Python package; the packaged Engine is still included. Python 3.10 or newer is required.


From a source checkout, install the wrapper and select a separately built Engine:


Shell
python -m pip install -e ".[speed]"
export VIGO_RUNTIME=/path/to/headless-runtime


VIGO_RUNTIME can name a complete headless directory or a built vigo.mjs file. A source .mjs needs system Node and its matching native kernel. See runtime selection for complete layouts and Windows usage.


2. Prepare the City


A City is a prepared directory built once from a static GTFS ZIP and an OpenStreetMap .osm.pbf. The Engine Boston tutorial lists where to download both. Save this as build.py and run it once:


Python
import vigo

with vigo.build(
    "./boston",
    gtfs="./data/MBTA_GTFS.zip",
    osm="./data/massachusetts-latest.osm.pbf",
) as city:
    print(city.name, city.revision_id)
    print("timetable covers", city.service_period())


Build runs the engine's Rust compiler, the same one behind vigo build and Studio, so a City built here is identical to one built elsewhere. In a terminal or notebook it prints each stage and the elapsed time; a Boston build takes about a minute. Missing input files are reported before anything starts. Build refuses to overwrite an existing City unless you pass replace=True. Add prepare_dates=["2026-10-05"] to compile the dates you will query into the City.


Build once; reopen the saved City with vigo.open() in later sessions. Do not call Build inside a query loop. Keep the entire directory, including its timetable and street files. If a prepared City predates the supported format, rebuild it from its original inputs into a new directory.


3. Run a journey query


Save this as route.py. The example requires Boston street coverage and a timetable active on October 5, 2026, as in the Engine tutorial. With another feed download, pick a date inside city.service_period().


Python
import vigo

with vigo.open("./boston") as city:
    result = city.route(
        [-71.11902, 42.37334],
        [-71.05524, 42.35227],
        depart_at="08:00",
        service_date="2026-10-05",
        max_walk_km=1.2,
        require_transit_ride=True,
    )
    if result.status == "ready":
        print(f"Journey: {result.duration_minutes:.1f} minutes")
        for leg in result.legs:
            print(leg["type"])
    else:
        print("No journey under the supplied constraints.")
    result.export("route-result.json")


Run it with the same interpreter used for installation:


Shell
python route.py


The first query starts the resident process and opens the required data. Further queries in the same with block reuse that process. Exiting the block releases it; returned Results remain usable.


4. Read and reuse the answer


duration_minutes is the selected journey duration. legs contains its timed steps and available geometry. Inspect warnings before using a path in a passenger-facing application. A blocked Result is a valid no-journey outcome; VigoError reports a failed operation.


Next, try arrive-by routing, a travel-time matrix, or walking and transit Reach. The batch workflow keeps failures separate from valid blocked results.

VIGO concepts in Python
VIGO Python 1.0.04 min readSource
On this page
CityScenarioQueryRouteMatrixReachResultTimePython
VIGO has four first-class concepts and three Query families. Build or open a City, optionally apply a Scenario, then retain the Result of a Query.


City -> Route | Matrix | Reach -> Result
  ^
optional Scenario


City


A City is a compiled mobility model built from GTFS and OSM. Its directory is one atomic unit containing the timetable, street model, and the data needed to open them quickly.


A named City may be rebuilt over time. Each build is an immutable revision. A Result records the revision it used.


city.revision_id identifies the build. city.built_at records when it was created. city.sources records its GTFS and OSM inputs. Moving the complete City directory does not change that identity.


Scenario


A Scenario is an immutable set of changes applied to exactly one City revision.


The shared VIGO model can describe:


  • proposed transit service changes;
  • one live transit state;
  • one supplied traffic state.


Query choices such as a walking limit, departure time, or time cutoff are not Scenario changes. A complete alternative GTFS source is another City revision, not a Scenario. Map geometry used to draw an edit is presentation data, not a transport change by itself.


VIGO checks a selected combination before running it. It never drops an unsupported change and quietly returns the unchanged City.


Python supports planned service changes in Reach and in Monte Carlo Route, Matrix and Reach, plus supplied traffic in Drive Route/Matrix. Python live-transit Scenarios, realtime transit Matrix, and realtime Reach are unsupported. Supplied traffic uses the shared native driving kernel and requires an engine that advertises that capability.


city.supports(query) and scenario.supports(query) return a Support value with a reason and available alternative when the selected context cannot execute a combination. This is not a complete data-validation pass; execution still checks points, dates, and runtime inputs. See the Python support table.


Query


VIGO has exactly three Query families.


Route


Find and explain travel between ordered points. Transport mode, depart-at, arrive-by, departure windows, waypoints, and batch requests are Route options.


Depart-at minimizes arrival time, then boardings, then walking. Arrive-by maximizes departure time, then minimizes boardings and walking among journeys arriving by the deadline, then actual arrival.


Matrix


Compute scalar travel time between one or more origins and destinations.


Both depart-at and arrive-by accept up to 100,000 pairs. Fixed departures share one forward scan per unique origin; fixed arrival deadlines share one reverse scan per unique destination. Arrive-by duration runs from the latest departure to the deadline, including destination waiting.


Reach


Compute where the represented network can travel within stated time limits. A Reach Result may be viewed as contours or reached streets.


Depart-at Reach spreads from an origin. Arrive-by Reach gathers toward a destination: it maps where a traveler can leave from and still arrive by a deadline, such as the homes that can reach a school by 08:30.


Reach is not Accessibility. Accessibility requires opportunities such as jobs, population, schools, or healthcare in addition to travel impedance.


Result


A Result is the immutable answer to one Query. Every Result exposes:


  • status;
  • Query inputs;
  • warnings;
  • timing;
  • City revision and Scenario name;
  • export methods.


Compare is an action on two compatible Results. It is not a fourth Query family.


Result status is only ready or blocked. A completed Matrix is ready even when individual rows are blocked. Python-side query validation raises InvalidQuery; unsupported combinations raise UnsupportedQuery; runtime validation and execution failures raise VigoError. Background work separately reports queued, running, ready, cancelled, or error through Job.status.


Compare uses retained values and checks family-specific structure; the caller must align dates, points, modes, and other study assumptions. A valid numerical difference does not establish that two Results answer the same question. See Results for comparison and evidence boundaries.


Time


VIGO keeps these durations separate:


  • Build: GTFS and OSM become a City.
  • Open: a City revision becomes ready for queries.
  • Compute: the selected Query runs.
  • End to end: caller submission through complete Result.


Repeated Route calls may reuse one open process. The answer is still computed for every call.


The wrapper's timing["endToEndMs"] ends before Result construction and export. Use an outer timer for the complete Python operation; see runtime measurement.


Python


Python
import vigo

with vigo.open("./city") as city:
    route = city.route("A", "B", depart_at="08:00", service_date="2026-09-04")
    matrix = city.matrix({"a": "A"}, {"b": "B"}, depart_at="08:00", service_date="2026-09-04")
    reach = city.reach("A", depart_at="08:00", service_date="2026-09-04")


The VIGO command line uses the same nouns: vigo build, vigo inspect, vigo route, vigo matrix, vigo reach, and vigo compare.


vigo capabilities reports the public API version and supported combinations. VIGO Python V1 supports the VIGO V1 engine with API 1.0, capability schema v3, and trace output. Runtime selection rejects other API versions and capability schemas.


Route and Matrix accept max_transfers=0 for at most one boarding, max_transfers=1 for at most two, and so on through 31. Omit the option (or use None) for no additional cap. It applies to both depart_at and arrive_by and all Matrix shapes. A finite cap with ordered transit waypoints is currently unsupported.
