What’s new in 1.0.0
4 min readSource
On this page
Building CitiesRouting and preparationRuntime and reproducibilityDependenciesDistribution
VIGO 1.0.0 builds reusable transport Cities from GTFS and OpenStreetMap and answers Route, Matrix and Reach queries through the native engine, command line, Studio and Python. API 1.0, City format 1 and Result schema 1 retain their existing meanings. Published Cities remain readable without rebuilding.


Building Cities


The engine builds Cities itself: vigo build and vigo build-scenarios take the compiler's options, print the same progress and manifests, and need no Node or npm. The GTFS and OpenStreetMap compilers moved from JavaScript into Rust. The compiler's build and build-scenarios run the engine's commands, Python's vigo.build() runs the engine executable directly, and Studio's imports run the same Rust compiler, and the Cities it writes are the ones the JavaScript compiler wrote: every table, metadata value, snapshot and hierarchy matched on the test fixtures, Boston and Washington, DC, and the published 0.5.0 reader opens them. Only the bytesSaved compaction diagnostic in network.json can be a few MB higher. On one Apple M2 with the same local inputs, Boston built in 48 s instead of 138 s, Boston with wheelchair routing in 42 s instead of 75 s, and Washington, DC in 100 s instead of 165 s.


Routing and preparation


Studio groups services with the same ordered platforms and access paths even when their GTFS shapes differ by small coordinate rounding. Each departure retains its own line, times and geometry. Express-to-local journeys can keep the express to a later shared platform when the same onward train remains catchable, with unchanged endpoint times, boardings and walking. Pickup, drop-off, transfer rules, published minimum connection times and the requested buffer remain enforced at the later platform.


Transit Route, Matrix and Reach use one exact connection scan for every City. Frequency templates without exact times depart every headway from each window's start. Stop-level transfer rules apply with GTFS specificity, a platform's own rule overriding its station's; route- and trip-scoped selectors are not applied.


Bicycle Route, Matrix and Reach use a turn-aware customizable contraction hierarchy. Shared rank sweeps evaluate departure and arrival grids, retaining each endpoint's private-road permissions. One relaxed sweep from the fixed endpoint bounds how far each grid cell searches for walking access; cells the path certificate cannot settle repeat with every walking candidate. Supported timed roads and turns are checked at entry. A cell or route whose only access is timed is bounded by a legal earliest arrival or latest departure, or proved unreachable, so it no longer widens every cell's search. The selected preference profile ranks paths while the result reports actual cycling, walking and waiting time.


Existing Cities remain readable. Local source-checked graph indexes can reuse the hierarchy when a worker opens a City. They keep the upward hierarchy and shortcut witnesses; opening rebuilds the remaining columns and weights exactly. The indexes are derived from the original City and store no route or surface answers. Studio includes Bike in Reach for both departure and arrival isochrones.


Scheduled and realtime journeys, bicycle preferences, driving traffic, wheelchair profiles, planned services and Monte Carlo analyses use the shared native computation layer. Planned services preserve arrival, dwell and departure times across adjacent service days. Wheelchair preparation connects accessible platforms without declared entrances and retains explicitly accessible ramps whose incline gives a direction without a numeric grade. Rebuild a City to apply these preparation corrections to existing inputs.


The bicycle hierarchy enforces the distance limit together with timing and access rules. Transit Matrix scans index endpoints by stop, scenario exclusions use one timetable pass, and Reach drops walking labels whose continuations cannot improve the surface.


Studio address search filters suggestions to the selected City’s prepared street extent, with timetable coverage as a fallback. Switching Cities or replacing their data invalidates the regional lookup. Missing coverage never triggers a global search.


Runtime and reproducibility


The engine supplies Studio's complete query fingerprint, including the City, scenario, waypoints, alternative selectors and applicable realtime snapshot. Street publication refreshes Studio's provenance independently of the timetable. Native responses enforce their byte limit for complete and fragmented lines, and busy City slots return a capacity error when the resident limit is reached.


Replacement processes prepare walking, bicycle, driving or timetable state directly. Studio prepares the mode selected in Route or Reach while the City opens, including the result-rendering binding. Reach and Matrix requests stay on a worker whose corresponding network is loaded. Replacement workers retain only mode and timetable selectors, never a user journey or surface. The public gateway rotates rate-limit buckets once per minute. Interrupted City builds wait for compilers to close before removing unpublished output.


A single-City stream or serve worker prepares in the background as soon as it opens: today's timetable, the pedestrian hierarchy, the driving network and the bicycle hierarchy. A first request waits only for the part it needs that is still preparing. Prepared modes stay resident; VIGO_PREPARE limits preparation to some modes, or none defers each to its first request. Studio's workers open with only the timetable, because Studio prepares the mode a visitor selects; an explicit VIGO_PREPARE still applies.


Dependencies


The release updates the npm and Rust dependency sets together. The maintained GroveDB bincode codec replaces the unmaintained upstream crate, using the existing fixed-width encoding for prepared access profiles.


Distribution


Engine, CLI, Studio and Python bundles are built from the same source commit for Linux x64/arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64. Release publication requires the platform checks, isolated Python wheel integration, City portability, container checks and artifact checksums. The Python package is version 1.0.0.


See the guide, Python guide, changelog and prepared-data contract.

Verification record
3 min readSource
On this page
What a release runsWhat the engine suites checkWhat passing does not establishReproduce locally
This record lists the checks every VIGO release passes and what they establish. It ships in the engine archive as AUDIT.md. Test results for a particular build are in its release workflow run; the archive's manifest.json names the source commit they ran on.


What a release runs


The release workflow builds the engine, the compiler, Studio and the Python wheels from one tagged commit, on Linux x64 and ARM64, macOS ARM64 and Windows x64, and runs on each platform:


CheckWhat it covers
npm run check:releasePublic-source and release-file rules, the documentation, the native kernels, Studio, security, the routing runtime and the transport atlas
npm run check:rust-workspaceModel and schema tests, algorithm tests, strict Clippy and the routing crate's dependency boundary
cargo test and cargo clippy -D warnings (standalone features)Engine unit tests and lints
npm run check:corpusA frozen corpus of routing cases with expected answers
npm run check:standaloneThe engine on public synthetic Cities: Route, Matrix, Reach, scenarios, Flex, realtime, wheelchair, bicycle, HTTP lifecycle, Monte Carlo, documentation examples, and the permanent prepared-data gate
scripts/package-standalone.py, test/check-standalone-package.pyBuilds the archive from an allowlist, hashes every file, and reruns the engine suites against the extracted executable with an empty PATH
npm run check:cli-packageThe compiler archive, extracted
npm run check:studio-runtimeStudio's packaged runtime
Python wheel checksUnit, lint, documentation and live integration against the bundled engine, without host Node
Container checks (Linux)The release image and Compose file, as in Deploy the routing engine


What the engine suites check


  • Routing parity. The engine and the compiler return the same public Results across both time directions, stop and coordinate endpoints, transfer caps, parent stations, sibling platforms, direct-walk policy, calendar exceptions, matrices, scenario surfaces, realtime fallback and source geometry.
  • Independent algorithms. Separate graph and timetable implementations, which never supply production answers, check walking and driving shortest paths, earliest arrival and latest departure, every stop pair at each boarding boundary, transfer rules and forbidden transfers. See Checking routing accuracy.
  • Inputs and outputs. Conflicting clocks, malformed fields, unknown or irrelevant options, invalid grids, unsafe index members and oversized inputs are rejected. Saved output replaces its target atomically.
  • HTTP lifecycle. Bounded connections, headers, bodies, queue and responses; read deadlines that small chunks cannot extend; slow bodies outside the worker; deadlines that stop and replace the worker, even when its input pipe is full; recovery after an idle crash. POSIX stop and crash injection is skipped on Windows.
  • Realtime. Freshness, trip identity, duplicates, cancellations, skipped calls, NO_DATA, invalid predictions, expiry, past-prefix removal and alerts, each with its diagnostics.
  • Traffic. Cache identity follows the actual edge weights, even when a caller reuses its snapshot key.
  • Documentation. Every request on the engine reference runs against the engine; response excerpts, flags, request fields and environment variables are checked against the executable and its source.


What passing does not establish


The checks use small public synthetic inputs. Passing them supports the tested model and interfaces. It does not establish:


  • real-world arrival accuracy, completeness of a source feed, or physical station accessibility;
  • fare eligibility beyond the published GTFS rules;
  • throughput, latency or memory on a particular City and machine;
  • behavior on platforms the release did not test.


Agreement between the engine and the compiler does not by itself prove their shared kernels correct; the independent checks address that, within their synthetic fixtures.


Reproduce locally


From a source checkout with the documented toolchain:


Shell
npm ci
npm run build:cli-runtime
npm run build:standalone
npm run check:standalone
npm run package:standalone
python3 test/check-standalone-package.py


Node and Python are development tools here; neither ships in the engine archive. A package built from uncommitted source is marked dirty: true in its manifest and is a development build.

Developer resources
2 min readSource
On this page
Build and understand the engineValidate behavior and performanceBuild on a small machineMaintain the documentation
Integrate VIGO through its public interfaces: the engine command line and HTTP API, the compiler, or VIGO Python. Studio's internal API and the native operations serve other purposes and are not stable integration boundaries.


Build and understand the engine


  • Contributing and checks
  • Architecture
  • How VIGO computes answers
  • Runtime limits and recovery
  • Local basemap


Validate behavior and performance


  • Routing accuracy checks
  • Performance measurement
  • Timetable query performance
  • Reproduce a service workload
  • GTFS support


A passing public synthetic fixture verifies the behavior it exercises. Use the test results of the exact build and platform when assessing an installation; an old test count is not a current release check.


Build on a small machine


npm run build:standalone and npm run build:rust-routing-kernel (and the scripts that call them) select low-memory Cargo settings when the detected physical or container memory is 4 GiB or less: one job, 16 code-generation units, no incremental compilation, no debug information and no LTO. When only available memory is low, they limit compilation to one job and keep the normal release profile. Unknown limits are ignored, and the selection is logged.


VIGO_BUILD_MEMORY=low forces low-memory settings and VIGO_BUILD_MEMORY=full keeps the release profile; the default is auto. Low-memory builds can run differently, so use full on a well-provisioned host for comparable benchmarks. A direct cargo build bypasses the selection. Changing modes rebuilds affected Cargo artifacts. node --test test/check-build-memory.mjs tests the detection. These settings reduce compiler memory; they do not guarantee a fit, and they do not change VIGO's runtime limits.


Maintain the documentation


Markdown is the source of the offline guide, docs/guide.html, which the engine serves at /, Studio opens under Settings → Documentation, and the engine archive includes.


FileRole
docs/guide.mdThe user guide: overview, install, quickstart, concepts, task guides, Studio, deployment, limits, troubleshooting, glossary
docs/guides/rust-standalone.mdThe engine reference; also the engine archive's README.md. Its json query=…, response=…, output=… and decoder=… blocks are executed by npm run check:standalone-docs
docs/guides/cli-only.mdThe compiler guide; also the compiler archive's README.md
docs/guides/*.mdMonte Carlo, resource limits and the public route planner
docs/reference/*.mdPublic results, methodology, walking evidence, the prepared-data contract and the verification record
docs/reference/api-schema.md, rust-standalone-native.md, docs/standalone-openapi.jsonGenerated from the Rust types by npm run docs:standalone; never edit by hand
docs/navigation.jsonPages, groups and order: each page renders a file, one section of a file, or several sections


Run npm run docs:build after changing a page, then npm run check:docs and npm run check:standalone-docs. The checks verify links and anchors, generated-file freshness, executable examples, and that every engine command-line flag, request field and environment variable is documented. Add to these files rather than creating a page per topic. Version history is in the changelog.

Architecture
8 min readSource
On this page
Build and openComputation ownershipCratesModule boundariesDesktop and NetworkStorage and verificationItinerary geometry and identifiers
Studio and the CLI share routing code; neither routes through the other. The public model is City → optional Scenario → Query → Result.


Studio renderer                       vigo command / Python wrapper
    │                                         │
Electron preload → utility process     CLI validation and output
    │                                         │
    └──────── shared City / query modules ─────┘
                          │
                 Rust timetable + street kernels
                          │
                   Result and diagnostics


Browser development uses loopback HTTP in place of the desktop memory channel, with the same handlers. The Studio HTTP API is internal; the stable programmatic boundaries are the engine and the compiler.


Build and open


Build validates GTFS and OSM in a staging directory, creates timetable and street stores, prepares required native indexes, and publishes a complete City atomically. A failed build preserves the previous City. SQLite owns durable source and build data; production path search does not query SQLite at each routing step.


Store admission accepts current formats. Obsolete source stores require a rebuild; merge, compaction, and index preparation cannot upgrade them in place. Compaction happens before transfer topology and access preparation, and retires indexes tied to the previous database generation.


Open validates identity and loads the data a query needs. Active-service timetable snapshots and directed station-access contexts can be retained with the City. Derived caches can be regenerated from compiled data; missing required street indexes require restoration or a source rebuild. Ride geometry is loaded and aligned only for selected trips. See performance for cold, reopened, and resident timing boundaries.


New City builds persist the Rust drive hierarchy and both free-flow metrics. Drive startup maps these artifacts; it does not rebuild the hierarchy. The CLI prepares only the requested mode, and Matrix streams prepare each mode on its first use. Missing required drive artifacts cause a rebuild/restore error. Older Cities marked with an ephemeral drive hierarchy retain their existing behavior until rebuilt from source.


Computation ownership


In this guide, CCH means Customizable Contraction Hierarchies, the prepared street index used to accelerate path queries. CSA means Connection Scan Algorithm, which scans timetable connections in time order. A frontier keeps competing feasible options, such as earlier arrival versus less walking. A witness is the path or journey supporting a computed cost. Materialization assembles its stops, legs, and geometry into the returned Result. Admission validates whether input data can be used; prewarming prepares it before a query, and resident state stays in memory for reuse.


Rust reads, indexes, aligns, and clips selected GTFS shapes in one native cache. A reusable 8 KiB output buffer holds the sampled leg; JavaScript copies only its displayed points into itinerary objects. Both runtimes default to a 64 MiB shape-cache budget and at most 1,024 shapes. JavaScript handles store lifetime, orchestration, and public interfaces.


OperationImplementation boundary
Transit RouteNative forward or reverse timetable search, directed street access, then selected-journey reconstruction
Walk / Drive RouteNative directed street search, CCH acceleration, and path geometry
Bike Route / MatrixTurn-aware bicycle CCH, shared rank sweeps and verified path geometry
Transit MatrixShared native forward scans per origin or reverse scans per destination; optional selected witnesses
ReachNative timetable propagation and walk, drive, and bicycle surfaces; JavaScript contours and Result shaping
ScenarioJavaScript validation and compilation of supported changes; native routing applies the compiled overlay


JavaScript owns request validation, identity resolution, orchestration, cancellation, and presentation. Rust owns active-timetable departure/transfer indexing, GTFS-Realtime overlays (trip updates, Service Alerts and timetable reconstruction, shared with the standalone engine), station path compilation, graph search, and timetable propagation; see the kernel implementation map. Source-feature omissions remain explicit in results; shared implementation alone does not prove correctness. Independent checks validate the declared model.


Crates


All Rust code builds from the root Cargo workspace.


CrateResponsibility
vigo-routeTimetable search: forward, reverse, Matrix and alternatives; scenario and realtime views; transfer and station operators; reusable scratch
vigo-formatReading service timetables, validating memory-mapped snapshots and writing the portable City layout
vigo-prepareCompiling GTFS stop_times into connections, including exact frequency expansion
vigo-gtfsGTFS-Realtime decoding
vigo-trafficTraffic input, including NDW DATEX II v3
vigo-modelThe public request and Result types, and the generated OpenAPI document
vigo-runtimeStreet, access and driving kernels, the standalone executable, and the Node adapter


The routing crate has no Node dependency, filesystem access, environment lookups, thread creation or untyped JSON. The executable and the Node addon share these implementations; Node records are generated from the Rust types. ZIP and CSV admission, source scoping, calendars, City publication and application orchestration remain in JavaScript.


npm run check:rust-workspace runs the model and schema tests, algorithm tests, strict Clippy and the dependency boundary. npm run check:compiler compares the connection compiler with retained normalized tables from the earlier reference compiler (test/fixtures/gtfs-connections-052.json), 80 seeded feeds, malformed-input rollback, City build equivalence, the frozen routing corpus and the permanent reader/writer gate. npm run profile:compiler -- --runs 3 --output output/compiler-profile.json profiles GTFS import on a synthetic or supplied feed; keep private inputs and measurements outside the repository.


Module boundaries


AreaOwnership
src/server/gtfs/Store schema, admission and identity; calendars, stop-access indexing and coordinate-access profile lifecycle; walking policy and plans; result assembly, realtime timetables, and network previews. The coordinator retains store lifecycle and native query orchestration.
src/server/runtime/route-worker-pool.mjsRouting-worker leases, cancellation, prewarming, and memory pressure. The API entry point supplies the worker URL so source and packaged execution resolve the same worker.
src/map/Network, journey, vehicle, and Reach feature builders; layer definitions, paint, and basemaps. VigoMap.tsx owns React effects, map events, and selection.
src/state/Studio state. Shell, City, service clock, Network, Route and Analyze stores hold state and actions; selectors derive shared values; runtime.tsx runs requests, leases and polling without rendering UI.
src/components/studio/Sidebar, City library and source controls, and route surface. Workspace panels read their own store slices; App.tsx arranges the shell.


These modules do not import their coordinating entry points. Public GTFS exports remain available through national-gtfs-store.mjs. Calendar caches still belong to each admitted store. Walking-anchor profiles remain private to the walking-plan module and are cleared when the coordinator invalidates their store. Realtime query symbols and weak timetable caches belong to the realtime module; decoded street-edge bundles retain one weak cache in the Reach feature module.


Stop projections use weak references to both the timetable and street record, retaining only the current access profile for each pair. Changing a profile replaces its projection; returning to an earlier profile recomputes it. Worker transfer failures reject the affected request and release the queue slot while preserving the worker for subsequent requests.


The remaining large files have tighter state coupling: GTFS import and query orchestration share store identity and cache lifetime; national-osm-store.mjs couples graph admission and native preparation; the Rust coordinate and timetable kernels share search workspaces and snapshot layouts. Split those along explicit state ownership boundaries, with routing, cancellation, and persistence checks, rather than moving arbitrary line ranges. Vendor code is maintained separately.


For current admission budgets, restart behavior, and test coverage, see runtime limits and recovery.


Desktop and Network


Studio uses a native City overview reader and native Reach boundaries. Per-route timetable analysis, vehicle interpolation and local search remain JavaScript.


public/main.mjs owns windows, menus, dialogs, and the vigo://studio resource scheme. public/preload.cjs exposes a small desktop bridge to an isolated renderer without Node access. Engine runs in a utility process; packaged Studio has no TCP listener. Packaging copies the shared public/ distribution once.


Desktop build tooling overrides @electron/asar's glob and minimatch with patched versions for cancelled traversal and pattern amplification. These are development-only dependencies. check:studio verifies archive contents, exclusions and unpack patterns through the packaging tool's resolved ASAR library. Remove the overrides when ASAR's dependency ranges include the patched versions.


Network shares one route/station selection across its tabs, map, and line diagram. Known feed namespaces resolve against the City timetable; ambiguous bare IDs cannot select an agency. Station scope includes platforms, while a platform keeps its own events. Observation refreshes do not move the map.


SurfaceOwner
Trip times and patternsAgencyTripTimetable, NetworkTimetable
Map and lineVigoMap, AgencyRouteLine
Station board and evidenceStopArrivalBoard, AgencyEvidence
Network overview and observation exportsAgencyPanel, observationExport.mjs
Route/vehicle timingsrc/agency/routeOperations.mjs


The Network service owns observation polling, timetable inspection, route and vehicle views, station boards and observation exports. Connection state lives in network.sqlite; explicit disconnects persist across restarts. Vehicle matching preserves service dates, including previous-day overnight trips.


Studio Reach retains packed reached-edge data, lazily reuses decoded coordinates across cutoffs, and serializes large map-source replacement. Changing a displayed cutoff does not require rebuilding the street graph. Runtime fixtures check map updates and rapid cutoff changes.


Storage and verification


The complete City directory is portable; individual databases and native files are implementation details. Studio library settings, drafts and feed connections are separate application state.


Use the contribution guide to choose checks. Routing fixtures verify feasibility and witnesses; desktop runtime fixtures verify interaction. Network checks include connection persistence, source replacement, access control, in-flight invalidation and preservation of legacy data. No fixture or build proves field accuracy.


Itinerary geometry and identifiers


Rust reads selected shape rows directly from SQLite into numeric buffers and builds a distance prefix and a hierarchy of bounds in unit-sphere coordinates. The bounds skip sections that cannot contain a nearer candidate, including across the antimeridian and near the poles. The matcher still retains up to 16 points within 1 km per stop, evaluates the original haversine distances and tie rules, and aligns the complete trip monotonically to disambiguate loops. JavaScript samples the selected range from a compact coordinate column using the existing distinct-point stride and 512-point limit. Shapes with consecutive duplicates also carry an index of distinct source positions. Range clipping uses two binary searches and visits only sampled positions; shapes without duplicates use source positions directly. Short ranges use a single bounded pass. Final duplicate cleanup and distance calculation share one pass over the newly materialized coordinates. Prepared shapes remain subject to the store's entry and byte budgets, including the coordinate column, distinct-position index, spatial index, and bounded native candidate cache. A read-only source connection has a 2 MiB SQLite page-cache budget and closes when its routing store is disposed or invalidated. No itinerary answer cache is introduced.


Plan identifiers retain the existing 64-bit hash and Unicode code-point semantics. Rust performs that arithmetic; identifiers are selection keys, not security digests. npm run check:accuracy includes differential tests against the previous JavaScript shape matcher and identifier arithmetic.
PreviousDeveloper resourcesNextLocal OSM basemap
Project/Developer resources
Local OSM basemap
3 min readSource
On this page
Import and geometryRuntime boundsVerification
Local OSM uses cartographic features retained in the City's SQLite street store. It does not query or load the pedestrian or driving accelerator. The /local-basemap endpoint returns roads and water in one GeoJSON collection. The former routing-edge renderer and its /local-streets endpoint have been removed.


Import and geometry


The importer first selects water multipolygon members, then includes their node references in the street import's existing selection and geometry passes. Untagged members are joined in either direction, and inner rings remain island holes. These temporary relation tables are dropped before publication. Map tables survive routing-store compaction and travel with the SQLite artifact; no external source file or sidecar is required at runtime.


Only motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, and tertiary roads are drawn. Links enter at zoom 12; lesser road classes never enter the basemap. The routing graph still retains its original walk/drive eligibility rules. Rivers, canals, water polygons, and directed coastlines are independent of routing permissions.


Geometry is rounded to six decimal places and simplified at three detail levels during import. Identical geometries share one stored row across levels; invisible levels are omitted. Line pieces contain at most 128 input vertices, and persisted geometry contains at most 8,000 vertices per feature. Water relations exceeding 200,000 input vertices, containing unsupported nested geometric members, or missing complete rings are skipped and counted in metadata. Oversized source ways are also skipped for display. Display geometry is never used for routing.


Coastal water follows OSM's land-left, sea-right direction. The query clips and joins shorelines, closes complete chains along the viewport boundary, and retains coastal islands as holes. A nearby shoreline supplies the side for views wholly on land or sea. Interior breaks suppress ocean fill rather than inventing a coast. The PBF header bounds, or the retained feature extent when the header omits bounds, limit coverage. This does not reconstruct missing ocean geography beyond a regional extract.


Runtime bounds


  • An SQLite R-tree selects the requested area, detail level, feature class, and zoom before loading geometry. Coastline searches do not scan unrelated roads.
  • Each request opens a read-only connection with a 4 MiB page-cache target and no memory mapping; it closes the connection after querying. This is a SQLite cache setting, not a total process-memory guarantee.
  • Responses contain at most 4,500 features and 80,000 vertices. Water has a separate half-budget so it cannot displace all roads. SQL sorts feature metadata and fetches geometry only after it fits the response budget.
  • Coastline assembly separately caps both candidate input and clipped geometry at 4,096 pieces and 80,000 vertices. Boundary joins use sorted crossings instead of scanning all crossings repeatedly. Island assignment has a containment-work budget; exceeding either geometry or work limits keeps bounded shoreline outlines and omits ocean fill.
  • The browser requests 18% padding around its viewport, reuses it for small pans, debounces moves, aborts superseded fetches, and discards geometry on City or basemap changes. A fresh OSM import invalidates the loaded geometry.
  • Worker updates are serialized with only the newest waiting viewport retained. City changes hide the old layers immediately and wait for active worker work before removing or reusing the source, preventing delayed geometry from the previous City from reappearing.
  • One GeoJSON source serves all five map layers. Its tile index stops at zoom 14 with a 32-pixel buffer and 0.75 simplification tolerance. Light/dark changes update paint without fetching geometry.
  • Responses report sampling and incomplete geometry. There is no city-wide JavaScript geometry cache or tile-provider fallback.


These limits bound retained feature data, not total Electron, worker, tile-cache, or GPU memory. Viewport queries run synchronously; an R-tree query over many matching features can still take longer than a small-city query. Full-region import and prolonged large-city use require separate memory and responsiveness measurements.


Existing street stores remain usable for routing. A store without localBasemap metadata returns needs-import with a fresh-import instruction; it cannot recover road classes or water from routing snapshots that omitted them.


Verification


Run npm run check:map, npm run check:osm-pbf, node test/check-city-build-equivalence.mjs, and node test/check-map-runtime.mjs. The basemap fixture checks road selection, lake holes, coastal islands, offshore and inland views, query budgets, pathological coastline clipping, R-tree access, compaction, and independence from routing snapshots. The Electron fixture renders both appearances through the local Studio protocol with all external HTTP requests blocked, overlaps updates with repeated City-source replacement, verifies that only the newest geometry renders, and checks source removal.


For manual visual review, the runtime fixture accepts VIGO_BASEMAP_PREVIEW_FILE pointing to a local GeoJSON response and VIGO_BASEMAP_SCREENSHOT_DIR for light/dark screenshots. Keep downloaded extracts and generated images outside tracked source files.

Measuring performance
7 min readSource
On this page
What the timers includePreparation and reuseNative timetable preparationCompare equivalent workCold service and street preparationResident routing and realtime updatesCompact street indexes and geometry
Measure the operation the caller waits for. Keep source data, City revision, query semantics, output detail, and status counts fixed when comparing runs.


For the shared native timetable workspace and a reproducible component comparison, see Timetable query performance.


OperationStartEnd
Build from raw filesInvoke vigo build with local inputs and a new output CityThe complete City is published and the command returns
Raw files to first answerThe same Build invocationThe first complete Query Result returns
Reopen a prepared CityStart a new runtime on a complete saved CityIts first Query Result returns
Resident querySubmit to an already open CityThe complete Result returns to the caller


Report downloads and runtime installation separately. State whether process startup, transport, export, and operating-system file-cache effects are included. A new process does not imply a cold filesystem cache; reading a saved Result is not a new computation.


What the timers include


  • network.json.timing describes compiler stages. totalMs begins inside the compiler after input/staging checks and ends before writing the manifest. It excludes process startup, shutdown, final City publication, and the first query. Stages may overlap; their durations cannot be summed into wall time. osmBuildMs can include waiting until the parent collects the worker result.
  • Route searchStats.queryMs measures the timed route-search and selected-journey work, including street access. It excludes fare annotation performed by the caller, final CLI decoration, transport and Result serialization. CLI routeMs / computeMs wraps routing, fare annotation and CLI decoration; it still excludes final serialization and transport.
  • materializationMs covers selected itinerary assembly. Its components include trip connection loading, metadata lookup, shape extraction, access/egress geometry, leg normalization and identity construction. Components need not sum to the enclosing timer. A geometry improvement is not automatically the same improvement in the complete response.
  • engineQueryMs measures native timetable work. For arrive-by, this includes reverse feasibility and forward selection; arriveByNativeQueryMs and forwardEngineQueryMs identify those components. Street access and geometry are outside that timetable total.
  • Matrix computeMs covers engine execution; requestPreparationMs and resultAssemblyMs describe caller preparation and row assembly. openMs reports mode initialization, including the first request of each mode in a stream. JSON serialization and transport require an external timer. Optional journey timings describe witness rendering, not independent searches or a share of batch time.


Use an external elapsed timer for complete Build and query latency. A small native search time does not establish the same user-perceived response time.


Fare parsing and localized display have separate costs. Whole-unit prices within the exact-integer fast path need no currency formatter; fractional and large prices still consult currency precision, and displayed labels still format currency symbols. Include the first fare-bearing result when measuring a fresh process. A preceding blocked route does not initialize every successful-route presentation path.


Preparation and reuse


Build includes import, required street indexes, stop transfers, station access, and publication. The first query may also compile its active-service timetable and align selected ride geometry. Report this cache-miss preparation separately from resident query time.


Portable binary timetable snapshots and prepared station access can be reused after moving the complete City. Timetable diagnostics distinguish loaded from written; a loaded snapshot reports compileMs: 0. New service patterns, changed walking policies, evicted caches, or older derived formats can require preparation. Missing required street indexes are errors, not permission to use a different graph.


Queries are recomputed. disableCache: true on transit Route/Matrix disables access/path caches while retaining the prepared City. Larger walking matrices may build temporary destination indexes; that setup belongs in the measured request.


Node Reach retains up to 64 next-departure schedule diagnostics per opened source store and active service context. This lookup preserves raw SQLite times and the inclusive 24-hour horizon; changing the service context clears it, and replacing the source creates a new lookup. It is immutable schedule metadata and remains available with disableCache: true. Reach still recomputes the timetable frontier and pedestrian surface. Measure first or changed departure clocks separately from repeated clocks; diagnostics.timetable.departureLookupMs exposes this cost alongside residentPrepareMs, search and surface timing. A faster repeated diagnostic lookup does not establish a faster native search or City opening.


Native timetable preparation


Standalone profile/trace output includes timing.timetableActivationMs, the time spent activating the service timetable during that request. A source preparation also reports timing.timetablePreparation with setupMs, sourceAndRealtimeMs, indexMs, and kernelMs. Setup includes calendar resolution and retiring the preceding timetable; source includes SQLite loading and realtime application. These scopes belong to execution and exclude public formatting, serialization, transport, and initial City opening. A reused timetable has no new preparation record. Profile scopes can overlap total execution; do not add them to it.


Rust constructs per-stop departure order, deduplicates transfers, expands station fallback links, and packs transfer adjacency. JavaScript resolves source IDs and passes typed arrays to the native preparation operator. This runs on active-timetable cache misses; loading a compatible persisted snapshot bypasses it.


Measure input marshalling and native preparation together when comparing the migration with the previous implementation. Keep SQLite reads, native search-index construction, snapshot loading, and resident query time separate. Preserved transfer ordering and snapshot layout do not by themselves establish a speedup. Filesystem lifecycle, source admission, and Result presentation remain JavaScript responsibilities.


Compare equivalent work


Record exact date/time, coordinates or stop IDs, walking speed and limits, boarding requirement, transfer cap, horizon, realtime snapshot, and output detail. Allowing a walk-only answer changes the workload. Separate ready, blocked, and error counts; a faster blocked result or a different journey is not an equivalent successful query.


For Build comparisons, hold raw inputs and compiler options fixed and compare compiled content; fresh revision IDs and build timestamps are expected. Performance checks complement accuracy checks, not replace them.


Cold service and street preparation


The native service reader opens the admitted SQLite source read-only and packs active connections directly into column buffers. JavaScript retains source admission and memory guards; Rust retains connection permissions, trip ordering, and discontinuity rules. A missing native reader is an error, not a JavaScript fallback. VIGO_ACTIVE_KERNEL_PERSIST=0 disables both reading and writing the active timetable snapshot when measuring compilation from source.


Prepared street graphs and CCH structures are validated concurrently during native construction. Validation still scans every required array. Path-query scratch distances use zero-filled storage with an encoded unreachable value, so the first path does not need to fill city-wide distance and predecessor arrays. These changes do not reuse previous route results.


Both persisted and in-memory Drive hierarchy construction use one 33-percent balanced four-axis flow cut per component. New City builds persist the hierarchy; opening that City loads it instead of repeating construction. Both retain every node and edge and use the same exact CCH search and distance certification; ordering can change the chosen witness between equal-cost paths. Arc ordering uses a shared stable counting sort. Native kernel diagnostics expose the hierarchy's arc count so preparation time can be evaluated alongside its size.


For a cold comparison, alternate baseline and candidate in separate fresh processes, include imports, graph opening, timetable compilation and result serialization, and compare route contents as well as latency. Keep immutable City inputs and hierarchy preparation policy identical. In particular, an in-memory drive hierarchy must be rebuilt on both sides; loading a saved hierarchy only on the candidate is not a cold code speedup. Report operating system page-cache control separately from application cache isolation.


Resident routing and realtime updates


For warm routing, retain the prepared City but disable access and path result caches. Verify the per-request cache diagnostics, rotate endpoints and departure times, and report native search separately from geometry materialization and whole-request time. Shared immutable indexes are preparation, not query answers.


Realtime measurements need two workloads: queries against an already prepared snapshot, and changed snapshots that force reconstruction and native indexing. Keep freshness, service date, applied update counts and fallback status in the retained evidence. Controlled updates on a real timetable measure computation; they do not establish live prediction accuracy. Compare reconstructed columns and route results, including cancellation and skipped-stop behavior.


Drive constrained-search buffers and traffic weights are allocated on demand. Report reserved bytes separately from resident memory: operating systems can back zero-filled allocations lazily, and allocator retention can obscure RSS changes after buffers are released. A normal CCH query should not allocate the constrained-search workspace merely to keep a kernel resident.


Compact street indexes and geometry


The v2 hierarchy stores seven aligned query columns. Its size without customization data is 104 + 16 * nodes + 12 * hierarchy_arcs bytes. Walking indexes use exactly this layout. Driving appends gzip-compressed input mappings for traffic updates; normal queries map the query columns without decoding the mappings. Inverse rank and arc tails are reconstructed only when customization needs them. Serialization uses a fixed 16 KiB buffer.


Transit shape coordinates and their distinct-point index remain native. Each selected Studio leg writes at most 512 points into an 8 KiB worker-local scratch buffer, then copies those points into its owned response. No full shape is exported or retained in JavaScript. The exhaustive clipping checks include loops, duplicate runs, signed zero, endpoint preservation, aliased endpoint views, and repeated buffer reuse. Shared output buffers are rejected at the native boundary.


Measure shape-cache bytes, temporary allocation, and whole-request latency separately. Reducing duplicate coordinates need not reduce timetable search time, and a hierarchy file reduction is not the same percentage reduction in the complete City.

Project/Developer resources
Timetable query performance
9 min readSource
On this page
Coordinate routes and materializationStandalone startup and output boundariesReproduce a kernel comparisonQuality checksStandalone query execution
The standalone Rust executable and Node interface use the same timetable kernel. Standalone transit Route requests obtain a journey through the shared Matrix kernel with one origin and one destination. Matrices can request scalar times or full journeys.


Journey construction allocates its scratch workspace lazily and retains it with the immutable timetable. Each source clears only the frontiers it touched; each boarding round visits only reached stops. Run generation tags separate rounds, sources, and requests, including wraparound. The workspace contains no cached answers. Changing direction, endpoint policy, or boarding limits still performs a fresh search. Replacing the timetable also replaces its scratch workspace.


Scalar Matrix queries prepare the common endpoint arrays once per batch and reuse the changing source or destination buffers. Validation and routing objectives are unchanged. Depart-at still shares a forward search per origin; arrive-by shares a reverse search per destination. Journey selection keeps the same dominance rules, run order, transfer rules, time horizon, and tie breaks.


For coordinate batches, journey rounds finish after every reachable target has attained its own exact scalar time bound. The final round completes before stopping, preserving boarding and walking ties. Targets without a route retain their blocked result. Selected-stop requests that permit terminal transfers keep the general round path. Endpoint projection also shares identical directed access searches within one batch, even when persistent endpoint caches are disabled; stop IDs remain part of the standalone endpoint identity. Each input still receives its own output row or column.


Arrive-by Route retains the scalar forward reachability envelope through successive capped and deadline certifications. Reuse requires identical origin and destination seeds, costs, departure, horizon, and terminal-transfer policies. Extending a deadline admits the remaining timetable events; contracting it keeps a conservative superset that exact rounds filter against the requested deadline. A new scalar search or a separately built forward envelope invalidates the retained identity. The reverse latest-departure search and exact deadline/boarding/walking certification still run.


Capped coordinate arrive-by searches first obtain the unrestricted latest departure and seek a forward witness at that same boundary. They accept the bound only when the witness reaches the deadline within the boarding cap; an unrestricted blocked result also proves the capped result blocked. Otherwise the existing layered reverse scan resolves the cap. A 1×1 Matrix uses this same certified bound before its unchanged journey rounds. Work counters include the proof and any fallback; no trip choice or tie criterion is removed.


Retaining scratch trades some resident memory for fewer allocations. Native workspaceBytes diagnostics include the journey arrays and their retained capacities. Scalar-only users do not allocate journey scratch.


The scalar point scan rejects strictly later arrivals before computing boarding and walking tie-breakers; equal arrivals still receive the full comparison. An epoch-scoped lower bound on stop arrival skips boarding searches when every label is in the future. It uses eight additional workspace bytes per stop and does not change prepared data. The preliminary unrestricted scan for a capped point query retains labels and its forward run envelope but omits predecessor writes and intermediate chain construction. Exact capped rounds still recover the final journey with the existing boarding and walking objectives.


For ordinary Node Route responses, the adapter passes only the plan diagnostic fields consumed by the shared Rust public formatter: realtime metadata, arrival reserves, and the service clock date. This avoids serializing and parsing unused search trees. Full journeys, alternatives, and geometry remain present; requested summary, profile, and trace responses retain their existing diagnostic input.


Coordinate routes and materialization


For capped fastest depart-at queries, the Node adapter permits the fused Rust call to return the selected access and egress witnesses, including walking geometry. The existing native guard uses this compact result only for certified one- or two-boarding routes. Uncapped queries, balanced preferences, departure-window alternatives, and arrive-by deadline certification retain the full candidate frontier. The change removes candidate conversion and subsequent path calls without limiting the search.


The standalone adapter retains immutable route metadata and trip-to-shape identifiers within each opened City. Journeys still reconstruct their active timetable stop sequence and geometry on every request. The metadata maps are bounded by the City's route/trip counts, are released with that City, and remain separate from endpoint or answer caches.


When opening an access context, the standalone stop projection parses only the normalized fields it consumes and validates JSON in skipped fields. Coordinate type checks and the null-coordinate exception for location types 3/4 remain unchanged. This changes reader allocations, not the portable City layout.


Reached-street propagation uses a monotone queue keyed by exact finite nonnegative floating-point duration bits. Equal-time entries use the existing walking-distance, node, seed, and witness ordering. A nonmonotone insertion falls back to the original heap. This does not round times, change walking budgets, or alter Pareto dominance. Node and standalone use the same operator. Compare full rasters and edge evidence, alongside measured execution and process memory, when evaluating queue changes.


Compiled GTFS shapes and their geometric alignment candidates are retained separately in a City-owned least-recently-used store, limited to 4,096 shapes and 256 MiB of estimated geometry storage, matching the Node interface's shape-cache limits. Lookups examine the most recently used entries first. This avoids the much smaller standalone cache repeatedly evicting geometry on varied city-wide workloads; the larger upper bound can increase resident memory. Sizes are accounted again after alignment grows candidate data. Oversized shapes are used for the current request and released. Timetable paths, realtime stop sequences, and selected shape slices are still reconstructed for each journey; the store does not retain route answers.


The standalone store also retains up to eight exact stop-to-shape alignments per shape within the same byte budget. The complete active stop coordinates, including their floating-point bits, form the key. A changed realtime stop sequence cannot inherit the scheduled alignment. Materialization copies only the selected shape slice. Point endpoint roles use the shared two-worker native executor. Batch endpoint evidence remains typed and is shared for identical request endpoints; it becomes JSON only when a response includes that evidence.


Generic street geometry keeps the original directed snap pairs, raw path distance, and tie rules. CCH path reconstruction shares one forward sweep across the candidate destinations for a source. Every destination still performs its exact backward sweep and shortcut reconstruction. The shared state is scoped to that batch call, so a subsequent source or metric never inherits it.


Standalone startup and output boundaries


The standalone City reader deserializes the used access-context fields directly into native structures and skips unused projections. Scheduled transit can load the compiler's portable active-service snapshot after checking database identity, access policy, active services, transfer projection, dictionaries, canonical array layout, and native kernel invariants. Missing or invalid optional sidecars fall back to the existing SQLite preparation path. Realtime and modified street-transfer policies use source preparation. timing.timetableSource exposes the selected preparation path; timing.totalMs still excludes process startup and initial City opening.


Rust Matrix defaults to full display and walking-evidence detail. Node Matrix returns compact timed witnesses. For a comparable analytical workload, request Rust journeyFormat: "compact" with includeJourneys: true, or request duration-only matrices from both. Compact changes response detail only: the same native journey search runs, with the same trips, boarding sequences, clocks, and transfer count. Full remains the default and the required format for geometry and walking-evidence consumers. The stream uses bounded 64 KiB serialization scratch instead of retaining another complete encoded response.


Forward and reverse batch bounds share one endpoint accumulator. Reverse scans minimize negated departure times with nonnegative access offsets, and stop once all nonempty endpoint frontiers have a bound that earlier connections cannot improve. Empty frontiers remain unreachable; an unreached nonempty frontier keeps the scan open. Directed terminal transfers and equal-time closure retain their existing semantics. This removes the former full-horizon scan for bulk arrive-by queries and the separate per-origin readout. Matrix still shares one forward scan per origin or one reverse scan per destination, so rectangular matrices can have different costs in the two directions.


cargo test -p vigo-route timetable::many::tests checks reverse batches against time-mirrored forward queries and scans forced to retain the entire horizon, including boarding caps, directed transfers, excluded trips, duplicate and empty endpoints, zero-duration connections, and reuse after a bulk query. The synthetic cutoff fixture examines fewer than 10 connections rather than at least 1,002. These are work counts for that fixture, not a production latency guarantee.


Full arrive-by journeys use a shared forward prefix bound before reverse journey rounds. Each requested origin is seeded at its already proven latest departure for that destination, including only its permitted initial transfer. The prefix scan ignores the boarding cap to remain optimistic, retains direct walking seeds, and permits post-ride transfers. Reverse candidates earlier than all reachable prefixes are discarded before transfer/frontier comparisons. The exact rounds still choose boardings, walking, actual arrival, and full witnesses. A conservative floating-point tolerance retains boundary-equal candidates.


The prefix pass reuses the many-target scan with endpoint-cutoff bookkeeping disabled: it needs all stops through the horizon. Its work is included in Matrix search counters. Prefix scratch is recomputed per destination and reused across requests; it does not cache answers.


Full depart-at journeys use the corresponding reverse suffix bound. Each destination is seeded at the latest of its exact earliest arrivals across the requested origins, allowing one conservative pass to serve all rows. It retains direct egress and the destination's permitted final transfer, ignores boarding caps, and includes walking into a first ride. The existing reverse scan reads out first-boarding deadlines for every stop without endpoint maps. A forward label after that stop's deadline cannot complete an optimal journey; runs departing after the same bound need not enter the boarding round. The bound is recomputed for every request, including when endpoints or direction change. Its scan and transfer work is included in the query counters.


opposite_bounds_preserve_complete_journeys compares complete witnesses with pruning disabled across fractional access costs, empty/duplicate endpoints, directed terminal transfers, boarding caps, transfer buffers, zero-time connections, unreachable prefixes and suffixes, and changes of direction on a reused kernel.


Reproduce a kernel comparison


Build each version with npm run build:rust-routing-kernel using the same toolchain and release settings. Save the earlier crates/vigo-runtime/vigo-routing-kernel.node under a separate path before building the changed version. Then run:


Shell
node scripts/benchmark-timetable-queries.mjs --reference /path/to/before.node --samples 51 --output /path/to/comparison.json


The script generates deterministic synthetic timetables with 256 and 4,096 served stops. It measures 1×1, 16×16, 1×128, and 128×1 requests in both time directions, with and without journeys and terminal transfers, using a three-boarding cap. Baseline and changed calls alternate execution order. Every call must preserve times, blocked cells, and full journey contents. Reports retain search counters separately because an optimization can reduce the work. They also include individual samples, medians, p95, native timing, and resident workspace bytes.


The outer timing includes Node-API argument/result conversion. Native timing excludes that conversion. Both exclude City loading, endpoint street routing, geometry, fares, JSON serialization, HTTP, and process startup. No answer cache is used; the prepared timetable and scratch memory remain resident. The first request for a workload is measured on the existing kernel and is not a cold-process or cold-filesystem measurement.


Quality checks


test/check-timetable-query-reuse.mjs compares a reused kernel with fresh kernels across changing endpoints, time directions, boarding limits, endpoint transfer policies, empty access, and invalid requests. Rust unit tests exercise generation wraparound and recovery after a journey-bound error. Run the existing native matrix, independent routing-accuracy, transfer, equal-time, and standalone parity checks as well: agreement between two adapters does not independently prove the shared kernel correct.


For workload measurements, use complete caller-visible Route and Matrix requests on representative prepared Cities. Alternate identical requests between resident baseline and candidate processes, exclude a stated warm-up round, retain all responses, and compare complete route semantics. Keep cold loading, street access, timetable search, journey/geometry construction, serialization, and transport separate. The standalone engine already moves request execution into Rust; additional migration should target a measured remaining cost and preserve each interface's supported behavior. Private City inputs and workload evidence belong in the private benchmark repository.


Standalone query execution


Capped coordinate point queries use the same destination-directed exact certifier as Node Route. Arrive-by first proves the latest departure, then certifies boardings, walking, and actual arrival within the deadline. Unsupported cases retain shared Matrix reconstruction; selected-stop and unbounded queries retain that path. Full geometry and walking evidence remain part of the response. Equal objective values can select different source-valid transfer stops; check source legs and objectives separately from byte equality.


Transit matrices group repeated endpoint identities before timetable search and journey construction, then restore every requested row and column. Coordinates and stop identity must both agree; different co-located stops cannot share permissions. Full and compact output remain explicit choices, and scalar requests retain their original dimensions.

Project/Developer resources
Runtime limits and recovery
6 min readSource
On this page
Memory and request admissionRecoveryTests with real execution
These limits and recovery rules apply to Studio's routing runtime and the compiler's Node workers. The engine's limits are in Server limits and Resource limits.


Memory and request admission


Studio's native runtime admits at most VIGO_NATIVE_CITY_MAX Cities (default 2, range 1–8), with at most VIGO_NATIVE_CITY_PROCESSES processes each (default 2, range 1–8). When all City slots are busy, a new City returns HTTP 503 with capacity_exceeded; idle slots can be reused. These count limits complement the native memory budgets. Complete and fragmented native response lines share a 256 MiB limit. Mode preparation uses street.prepare, bike.prepare, drive.prepare or timetable.prepare, without retaining or replaying journeys.


Each native request follows one serving contract:


  • Admission. A request already cancelled, or for a City whose files are being replaced, is refused before any City is opened, evicted or started. An admitted request reserves a count and an encoded-byte permit, globally and for its City, and returns them however it ends. With no permit left the request fails at once with HTTP 503 and VIGO_NATIVE_OVERLOADED, marked retryable; nothing queues without bound. The VIGO_ROUTE_MAX_PENDING/VIGO_ROUTE_MAX_QUEUED limits below belong to the separate preparation pool, not to these requests.
  • One deadline. VIGO_NATIVE_QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS (default 600,000) is the request's whole budget from admission: waiting, a process start and one automatic retry all spend it. A request that expires while waiting leaves the queue without stopping a process; only the request a process is computing can stop that process.
  • Dispatch. Waiting work stays in its City's queue and goes to the first ready process that is free, including one that has just started; a request already written to a process is never moved. Work waiting behind busy processes starts another one, up to the process limit. Point routes go before Matrix and Reach analyses, which may be passed over at most four times. A request waits up to VIGO_NATIVE_AFFINITY_WAIT_MS for a process that has its travel mode loaded, then takes any idle process, which loads it first.
  • Generations. Replacing a City's files in the same library is a two-phase fence (withRetiredRouting): the City starts a new generation and its processes exit, then the files are replaced, then the City is released. Admitted work does not fail: waiting requests, and requests arriving meanwhile, wait until the release and then run on the new generation; a request the retirement stopped mid-computation runs once more there. Each stays within its own deadline. A failed replacement or its rollback releases too, and a release that never comes ends after VIGO_RETIRE_HOLD_MS, when the held work fails as being updated. The preparation pool follows the same rule for its route analysis and preparation jobs. A caller that knows which City it replaces (the wheelchair City's publish) names it by root, so its parent City is never stopped. Switching library instead resets the native runtime and the preparation pool: everything admitted before is refused, and work begun under the old library (a request still on its way, an import, a warm-up) is refused when it reaches either runtime, so it never reopens an old City. Both keep serving the new library without a restart.


ControlDefaultSupported range
VIGO_NATIVE_MAX_PENDING256 requests waiting or running1–100,000
VIGO_NATIVE_MAX_PENDING_BYTESCapacity ÷ 64, between 16 and 256 MiB1 MiB–4 GiB
VIGO_NATIVE_CITY_MAX_PENDING128 per City1–100,000
VIGO_NATIVE_CITY_MAX_PENDING_BYTESHalf the global byte limit1 MiB–4 GiB
VIGO_NATIVE_RESPONSE_BUDGET_BYTESCapacity ÷ 8, between 256 MiB and 2 GiB1 MiB–16 GiB; never below one response line
VIGO_NATIVE_AFFINITY_WAIT_MS5001–60,000
VIGO_NATIVE_RESTART_BUDGET6 process starts per City in 30 seconds1–100
VIGO_RETIRE_HOLD_MS300,000 ms a City or store waits for its replacement to finish1,000–3,600,000


The response budget counts native answers being received and decoded across every process. The first answer being received always finishes; others pause their output while the total is over budget. GET /api/health reports nativeRuntime.admission, responses and counters (overload refusals, expiries, retries, process starts and requests refused after a retirement or reset).


The Node routing-time validator has explicit interface bounds: Studio accepts whole minutes from 0 through 1799, and GTFS orchestration through 2880. The native public request schema accepts seconds through 71:59:59. Tests retain these boundary distinctions. Engine and Python documentation readers ship independently; their shared Markdown subset is checked for rendering parity.


The runtime uses the smaller of host RAM and Node's reported container limit to choose its default budgets. Configuration accepts finite positive integers; invalid values use the default, and valid values are clamped to the supported range. Zero does not disable the timetable byte guard.


ControlDefaultSupported range
VIGO_ACTIVE_KERNEL_MAX_BYTESOne eighth of capacity, between 64 MiB and 2 GiB1 MiB–16 GiB
VIGO_ROUTE_MAX_PENDING128 dispatches and, separately, 128 preparation lifecycles1–1,024
VIGO_ROUTE_MAX_QUEUED32 jobs per worker1–256
VIGO_ROUTE_WORKER_HEAP_MBOne eighth of capacity, between 128 and 2,048 MiB64–8,192 MiB
VIGO_ROUTE_JOB_TIMEOUT_MS900,000 ms1,000–3,600,000 ms
VIGO_ROUTE_WORKER_RSS_BUDGET_BYTESOne eighth of capacity, between 64 MiB and 2 GiB64 MiB–reported capacity


Timetable admission counts the active service slice before allocating native arrays, estimates its size, and checks retained bytes after construction. Realtime reconstruction estimates the resident scheduled view, rebuilt arrays and replacement calls before native compilation against the same budget. Default cache budgets scale with capacity.


The pool rejects excess work with status 503. Capacity waits have a deadline, and a worker watchdog requests termination when an operation exceeds its deadline. Under memory pressure the pool avoids adding a second City until an unleased idle worker can be retired. Worker diagnostics expose limits and pending counts. Shutdown wakes waiting requests and permanently closes the pool.


Within queued query work, Studio prioritizes point Route, departure-window, and street Route requests. An older analytical job runs after at most four point-query bypasses. Preparation and unknown operations preserve their queue order, and running native work is not preempted. Worker diagnostics expose maximumPointBypasses.


These are admission and retention safeguards, not a hard whole-process memory limit. V8's worker heap limit excludes native arrays and mapped street data. Imports, realtime reconstruction, result assembly, and serialization can still have temporary allocation peaks. The RSS check cannot interrupt a native allocation already in progress. A native call must return before thread termination can complete; operating-system memory exhaustion remains possible. Street and timetable budgets must be considered together for large Cities.


Recovery


A routing-thread failure rejects its active and queued work, waits for termination, and reopens authoritative City data for a subsequent request. Structured-clone failures reject only the affected job and leave the worker usable. No failed query is converted into a fabricated journey.


Studio keeps its window when the Engine exits. It allows three starts within a rolling minute, including the initial start, with increasing restart delays. Startup has a 30-second deadline. Once the restart budget is exhausted, a later request can try again after the rolling window permits it. Engine startup failure does not prevent the window from opening. Pending requests fail rather than being replayed automatically, because some requests change stored data. Studio admits at most 128 Engine requests, including those waiting for startup. When the Engine is unavailable or the restart budget is exhausted, desktop API requests return a structured 503 response. The interface can show the failure without waiting for an unresolved protocol request.


Packaged Engine environment filtering lives in public/engine-environment.mjs. Studio supplies its own application-data path after filtering so startup and recovery use the same configuration directory.


Tests with real execution


test/check-national-runtime-isolation.mjs builds real GTFS and OSM inputs and uses the production worker and native kernel: it verifies exact journeys after thread termination, rejects a 50,000-trip input under a 4 MiB budget, rejects an oversized realtime reconstruction while scheduled routing keeps working, and checks overload and shutdown. test/check-engine-recovery-runtime.mjs runs the Electron entry point, kills Engine processes, and checks health, the restart budget and the subsequent 503. These checks do not establish other-platform behavior, live-feed accuracy or immunity to memory exhaustion.

Project/Developer resources
Service benchmarking
2 min readSource
Use a retained NDJSON request file containing public Route, Matrix, and Reach requests. Each line includes kind, the City or scenario selection supported by your service, the service date, and all routing constraints. Keep the file and prepared City together with their source checksums.


Shell
node scripts/benchmark-service.mjs \
  --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --requests queries.ndjson --output results.json \
  --rounds 20 --concurrency 4 --warmup 1 --city ./city


Set VIGO_API_TOKEN if the service requires authentication. The benchmark does not write the token to its report and refuses to overwrite an existing result. It calls the service's /v1/route, /v1/matrix, and /v1/reach endpoints.


The report retains every measured call, warmup calls, request-file hash, runtime capabilities, client platform, and optional unique-file City storage. Latency includes queueing, HTTP, response transfer, and JSON parsing. Quantiles use nearest rank. Successful results, valid no-journey results, HTTP failures, overload, service unavailability, timeouts, invalid responses, and transport failures are reported separately. Errors during warmup also fail the run.


For a cold-start measurement, start a fresh service and use --warmup 0 --rounds 1. Measure readiness separately from the first query. For sustained use, retain the same workload and increase rounds; report how much the workload repeats and whether caches are enabled. Compare equivalent inputs, constraints, output detail, hardware limits, and runtime builds.


This replay is closed-loop: each client sends its next request after the previous one completes, so offered load falls when the service slows. To measure behavior at an independent arrival rate, use the open-loop companion against a privately started service:


Shell
python3 scripts/stress-http.py --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --requests queries.ndjson --output load-20.json \
  --rate 20 --duration 60 --max-inflight 32 --timeout 10 --slo-ms 250


It schedules arrivals at a fixed rate, caps its own in-flight requests and counts arrivals it could not send instead of queueing them invisibly. The report gives offered and completed arrivals, overloads, timeouts and latency from scheduled arrival. Only loopback targets are allowed unless --allow-remote is given, and it never overwrites a report. Raise the rate until successful arrivals within the SLO stop rising, and measure server memory and CPU separately.


City storage counts each file identity once, including shared scenario directories. It is logical file size, not physical APFS clone allocation. Server memory must be measured at the service: retain process-tree RSS/PSS or cgroup memory samples at startup, first query, repeated and concurrent queries, scenario switches, and peak large-output requests. Include the full application stack when claiming a deployment budget. The benchmark client's memory is not server memory.


Use public synthetic fixtures for CI and caller-owned Cities for operational acceptance. A short replay establishes behavior for that retained workload; it does not establish production reliability across unobserved traffic. See upgrading for installation and rollback checks.

Source layout and delivery
1 min readSource
All Rust code builds from the root Cargo workspace and Cargo.lock; see Crates. The vendored CCH dependency stays isolated with its license and notices. src/ contains Studio, its application services and GTFS and OSM import. Build outputs live in the root target/; do not add a nested lockfile or target tree.


CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs inside the Release workflow, or when started by hand; pushes and pull requests start no workflows. It runs source, documentation and Rust workspace checks, the Python package checks on Python 3.10–3.13 and three operating systems, and the engine, compiler, Studio and live Python suite on Linux. One Release workflow, started by the v<VERSION> engine tag, reuses CI's source and Python checks, then builds and tests the engine, the compiler, Studio and the Python wheels on all four platforms from that commit, packages the tested executable, checks Cities built on other platforms, and verifies the Linux containers before attestation and publication. Release container checks use deploy/Dockerfile.release and the verified archive; deploy/Dockerfile builds from source.


Within one unchanged CI job, VIGO_USE_BUILT_RUNTIME=1 reuses the runtime built earlier in that job and fails if a binary is missing. Never use it after editing Rust or embedded documentation; local builds stay source-checked by Cargo.

Bicycle implementation
2 min readSource
VIGO supports an optional bicycle graph in bike_nodes, bike_edges, bike_turns, and bike_way_turns tables inside the existing street database. Existing readers ignore these tables; no existing field, snapshot or format identifier changes. CLI builds opt in with --street-modes=walk,bike or --street-modes=walk,drive,bike. Studio OSM imports include bike streets.


The bicycle engine customizes one turn-aware contraction hierarchy for the selected profile, speed and stress limit. Ordinary movements use scalar shortcuts. Dated entries and endpoint-only permissions narrow the shortcut choices. When time or metres constrain a path, the same rank sweeps retain the necessary undominated travel time, preference cost and distance states. Endpoint projection uses the road segment index, and verified pedestrian connectors share the pedestrian hierarchy with unrounded distance weights.


A source-bound hierarchy cache can reuse the upward topology and shortcut witnesses on process start; opening it rebuilds the remaining columns and weights exactly. It contains graph data only. The original City remains the source of truth; its prepared files and portable layout do not change.


Bicycle Reach first bounds every cell's walking access with one relaxed hierarchy sweep from the fixed endpoint: a cell searches only as far as a bicycle node could still beat its best candidate. Cells whose minimum the path certificate cannot settle repeat with every walking candidate.


Preference cost is distinct from physical travel seconds. The default balanced and quiet profiles penalize traffic exposure; fast minimizes estimated travel time. Mapped surfaces and incline change speed. Dismount segments use walking time and are materialized as walk legs with geometrySource: "osm-dismount". Off-network coordinate connectors remain unverified walks. Bicycle Reach supports both departure and arrival queries. Bikes-on-transit, bike sharing and elevation rasters are outside this model. Unhandled relation shapes are counted in diagnostics.


All street modes estimate travel duration. A dated bicycle request also uses the City's time zone to evaluate supported weekly road and turn permissions at the moment of entry. When the request has no usable service clock, the engine excludes timed roads and applies conditional turn restrictions conservatively. Walk uses a static pedestrian graph; Drive can apply an admitted traffic snapshot to its static road metric.


The importer follows the OSM access hierarchy. Trunk roads retain explicit bicycle restrictions and motorroad exclusions; their classification alone does not make them motorways. Movable gates inherit the admitted way's access unless private, locked, or time-restricted. Mandatory separate cycle paths (bicycle=use_sidepath) exclude the roadway. These portable defaults are not a country-specific traffic-law model.


Run npm run check:bike, the Rust bike::tests, and npm run check:format-050. The latter checks that the published reference reader can open a newly written City with the optional bike tables.


Valhalla's bicycle costing documentation and elevation model provide feature references. VIGO's weights are its own documented heuristics. Passing synthetic regressions does not establish route-quality or performance parity with Valhalla, GraphHopper, or BRouter. Comparative evidence belongs in the separate benchmark workspace.
